Chapter Five Hundred Eighteen

Romans 16:2–4 · Phoebe, Prisca, and Aquila · The Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 16:2–3 “that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: that you receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of saints, and that you stand by to help her in any business in which she might have need of you; for she has also been of great assistance — a patroness — to many, including myself. Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus.

Romans 16 divides into three paragraphs: apostolic salutations (verses 1–16), the exception to honor code function (verses 17–19), and the concluding paragraph, the ultimate triumph of the royal family (verses 20–27). The chapter's governing theme is the Royal Family Honor Code — the operational standard of the believer's life as a member of an eternal aristocracy. Chapter 518 completes the study of Phoebe (verse 2) and opens the study of the married couple Prisca and Aquila (verses 3–4), drawing from both a sustained presentation of what mature Christian womanhood looks like and an introduction to the honor code itself.

I. Concluding Principles from the Study of Phoebe (Romans 16:2)

Verse 2 yields a cluster of doctrinal principles about the design and function of the woman in the divine order. Phoebe, the deacon of the church at Cenchreae and the bearer of the Epistle to the Romans, exemplifies mature Christian womanhood in the single state. The following principles are extracted from the text.

First, just as believers are designed by regeneration to respond to God, women are designed by creation to respond to man. The responding woman is the greatest of all creatures, while the reacting woman — the woman who rebels against her created design — is the most destructive. This is not because the world belongs to the man in an absolute sense, but because the woman's role within that order requires greater moral courage and places greater demands upon her character.

Second, the woman is under the authority of the man, yet she plays a far greater functional role than is commonly recognized. More is demanded of the woman than of the man, precisely because her influence upon the man and upon the environment of human society is so extensive. The woman who fulfills her created role is the greatest single civilizing force in human history.

Third, the old sin nature operates differently in the woman than in the man. The pride function of the woman's old sin nature is more subtle and more complex than that of the man. Subtlety and cunning, which are the characteristic strengths of the woman's mind, become the characteristic distortions of the woman's old sin nature when that nature is in control.

Fourth, the woman has the potential to be uniquely magnificent as the glory of the man (1 Corinthians 11:7). That potential becomes a reality only through regeneration and sustained advance in the plan of God toward spiritual maturity. Phoebe is the exemplar: a mature believer whose doctrine-resident soul gave her the capacity to provide comfort, encouragement, and inspiration of soul to the Apostle Paul in a way that no one else could. She exercised hospitality, honorable companionship, and noble encouragement — everything that is great in Christian womanhood: honor, integrity, maturity, and the capacity to bless the environment she inhabited.

Fifth, while Phoebe represents the best in the single state, the next salutation represents the best in the union of man and woman in marriage. The passage moves from the magnificent single woman to the magnificent married couple.

II. The Integrity of Prisca and Aquila (Romans 16:3)

Verse 3 reads in the corrected translation: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus.” The verb is the aorist active imperative of

The verb is the aorist active imperative of aspázomai (ἀσπάζομαι), meaning to greet, to pay respects to. The constative aorist contemplates the action in its entirety and refers to a momentary act of greeting. The active voice: Paul produces the action by writing this greeting. The imperative mood is the imperative of entreaty, not command — it carries the force of a warm personal request rather than a formal directive.

A. Prisca: The Woman Named First

The accusative singular direct object from the proper noun

The accusative singular direct object from the proper noun Priska (Πρίσκα) is the form used by Paul consistently. The diminutive Priscilla appears in the Acts narratives. Priska is the female name of the Acilian gens, one of the great patrician families of Rome. The name itself signals Roman aristocracy. She is named before her husband in four of the six New Testament references to this couple — a consistent and deliberate ordering that signals her exceptional prominence in the early church.

Prisca's profile is threefold. First, she is a mature believer who had cracked the maturity barrier. Second, she is a Christian wife who recognized and sustained the authority of her husband in every situation — when he traveled, when he was driven into exile, when he planted churches in foreign cities, she was in full accord with his decisions and provided the moral courage to sustain them. Third, she was a woman of exceptional intelligence who was capable of instructing the brilliant Alexandrian preacher Apollos in the fuller dimensions of church age doctrine.

Regarding the instruction of Apollos: Acts 18:24–26 records that Apollos was an eloquent man, mighty in the scriptures — but acquainted only with the baptism of John. He was one dispensation behind, having no knowledge of church age doctrine. When Prisca and Aquila heard him in the synagogue at Ephesus, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. Aquila contributed the Jewish doctrinal foundation; Prisca contributed the church age categories. Together they brought Apollos fully into the current dispensation. This is one of the most remarkable instances in the New Testament of a woman functioning as a doctrinal instructor.

B. Aquila: The Eagle

The accusative singular direct object Akulan (Ἀχύλαν) is from the proper noun Akulas (Ἀχύλας), meaning eagle. Aquila was a Jew from Pontus, a tentmaker by trade. When the Emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome in AD 49 — an event recorded by Suetonius in connection with disputes over one “Chrestus” — Aquila brought his wife to Corinth. The name Aquila is a Roman name; many Jews who settled in Rome adopted Roman names for professional and social purposes. His name indicates he had been a slave in the household of the Roman senator Aquila Pontus, and upon gaining his freedom, he took his patron’s name as his own.

Paul first encountered Aquila and Prisca at Corinth (Acts 18:2). Because they shared his trade as tentmakers, Paul lodged with them during his extended residence in Corinth. When Paul departed for Syria, Prisca and Aquila accompanied him as far as Ephesus (Acts 18:18), where they became pillars of the church. After the death of Claudius and the accession of Nero, restrictions on Jews in Rome were lifted, and Prisca and Aquila returned to Rome, where they opened their home as the meeting place for one of the local churches — the earliest organized assembly in the city. When Paul was imprisoned in Rome a second time, they had again returned to Ephesus, and Paul included them in his final greetings (2 Timothy 4:19).

C. Fellow Workers in Christ Jesus

The phrase “my fellow workers” renders the accusative plural direct object from the noun sunergos (συνεργός), meaning co-worker, fellow laborer. It stands in apposition to Prisca and Aquila, which is why it appears in the accusative case. The possessive genitive singular from egō (ἐγώ) gives the sense “my” co-workers. The locative of Christos and Iēsous — in Christ Jesus — identifies the sphere: royal family, functioning as a team within the body of Christ. No communicator of doctrine is an island. The function of the ministry requires sunergos: team members who are essential to the work.

Prisca and Aquila are a monument to three categories of love functioning simultaneously. They had category one love — occupation with the person of Christ, which gave their marriage its deepest foundation. They had category two love — maximum personal love for each other as husband and wife. And they had category three impersonal love — a doctrine-based capacity to love all believers in their sphere without partiality. Their home was a haven for every member of the royal family who came within their orbit, not because of personality or sentiment, but because doctrine resident in the soul had given them a great capacity for life and a great capacity for love.

Here is a marriage between a Jew and a Gentile that was not only the epitome of domestic compatibility, but a marriage that established the record for personal and impersonal love in the early church. Both husband and wife had cracked the maturity barrier — a rare combination. Together they functioned as the closest of friends to the Apostle Paul, who was himself the most discerning judge of character in the New Testament church.

III. The Royal Family Honor Code — Introduction (Points 1–2)

The salutations of Romans 16 are not a mere courtesy list. They are a sustained illustration of the Royal Family Honor Code in operation. Having studied Phoebe and now Prisca and Aquila, the text creates the occasion to present the honor code systematically. The following points constitute the beginning of that presentation.

Point 1 — Definition and Description

All aristocracies have standards, and those standards are called an honor code. At salvation, every believer receives two things that constitute permanent aristocratic standing: the imputation of divine righteousness, and union with Christ. These two facts make every believer a member of a permanent and eternal aristocracy — the royal family of God — an aristocracy that will never be destroyed and never disintegrate.

Human aristocracies rise through merit, virtue, and honor, and they inevitably face the problem of maintaining their standard across generations. The mechanism for maintenance is the honor code. What the honor code is to aristocracy, Bible doctrine functioning through the grace apparatus for perception is to the royal family of God. The honor code of the believer is not an external set of behavioral rules imposed from outside. It is the expression of divine righteousness already imputed to the believer, working outward through doctrine resident in the soul.

The central principle of point one is this: right thinking results in right motivation, and right motivation results in right function. Right function is the basic concept of the Royal Family Honor Code. It is based upon the perception of doctrine — the more doctrine resident in the soul, the more consistently the believer is able to function in a manner compatible with his aristocratic standing. Accidental right function is possible for anyone. Consistent right function requires a code — a standard internalized through sustained doctrine intake.

The honor code lines up with the plan of God for the Church Age believer: the advance to maturity through phases X, Y, and Z, culminating in the sixth divine imputation — the imputation of escrow blessings — which glorifies the Lord Jesus Christ. The ultimate function of the honor code is to glorify Christ and to receive the imputation of divine blessing. There is a direct relationship between the honor code and prosperity, as stated in verse 20: “now the God of prosperity be with you all.”

Morality is not the Christian way of life. Morality is the function of the laws of divine establishment and can be achieved by any unbeliever. The Christian way of life is something categorically greater — it is the honor code of the royal family, operating through the filling of the Holy Spirit and doctrine resident in the soul. The word “saint” (

The word “saint” (hagios, ἅγιος) captures this honor code status. The believer is not primarily a moral person; he is a set-apart person, a member of the royal family of God, functioning under a code of honor commensurate with that standing.

Point 2 — Freedom, Privacy, and the Priesthood

The honor code must begin somewhere, and it begins with the doctrine of the privacy of the priesthood as the operational expression of freedom. The Royal Family Honor Code recognizes freedom and emphasizes privacy.

Freedom is not an isolated concept. It is part of a system that has four essential components, all of which stand or fall together:

• Authority — without authority, freedom collapses into anarchy

• Freedom — the sphere within which the individual operates under authority

• Privacy — without privacy, freedom does not exist

• Property — without property, neither privacy nor freedom can be sustained

This four-part structure applies equally to the laws of divine establishment and to the Royal Family Honor Code. Establishment authority encompasses both the divinely ordered institutions of human government, family, and nation, and the spiritual authority delegated through the word of God to the pastor-teacher and to the spiritual gifts of the body. The privacy of the priesthood is the application of the freedom-privacy-property complex to the individual believer's life before God.

The privacy of the priesthood means that every believer has the right to live out his life before the Lord without interference, pressure, or distraction from other believers. The operative principle is: live and let live. This principle, rooted in the laws of divine establishment, is carried over without modification into the Royal Family Honor Code. Its corollaries include:

First, every believer has the right to assemble in the local church regardless of his occupation, social standing, or personal history. The pastor's function is to teach doctrine, not to manage the external lives of his congregation. Doctrine, once resident in the soul, will produce its own standards and norms in the believer who applies it — without coercion from any human authority.

Second, the property of every other person is inviolable. The honor code of the royal family treats the property of others as sacrosanct. This is not merely a legal principle but a reflection of the fact that property is the material expression of another person's freedom and privacy. To disregard another's property is to disregard his standing as a free person and as a fellow priest before God.

Third, the privacy of the priesthood demands that every believer approach the word of God objectively, without the distraction of others monitoring his reaction to the teaching. Objectivity in doctrine reception requires that no one be watching to see whether a passage “got” to another person. The moment a believer becomes conscious of being observed, he becomes defensive, and defensiveness destroys objectivity. Without objectivity, doctrine cannot reach the right lobe and cannot be metabolized into

Without objectivity, doctrine cannot reach the right lobe and cannot be metabolized into epignosis (ἐπίγνωσις), the full exact perception required for spiritual growth.

Fourth, the privacy of the priesthood demands the avoidance of gossip, maligning, judging, and implacable criticism. These mental attitude sins are not merely unpleasant social behaviors — they are violations of the priesthood of another believer. The divine discipline that accompanies them is commensurate with the gravity of the violation.

Fifth, the honor code demands toleration for non-essentials. Many things about which believers have strong opinions are not doctrinal essentials. The honor code requires that great latitude be extended to all varieties of opinion, lifestyle, and personal standard that do not bear directly on doctrine. The essential is doctrine; the rest is secondary.

Point three of the honor code — impersonal love — will be taken up in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighteen

1. Phoebe represents the maximum in single Christian womanhood. Her doctrine-resident soul gave her the capacity to provide Paul with comfort, encouragement, and inspiration that no one else could supply. She is the exemplar of the woman who fulfills her created design through spiritual maturity.

2. Prisca is named before her husband in four of six New Testament references. This is not an accident. Paul's consistent ordering reflects Prisca's exceptional prominence in the early church — not in violation of the authority structure, but as evidence that within it, a mature woman can achieve the maximum in Christian function.

3. Prisca and Aquila are the paradigm of the mature married couple. Both had cracked the maturity barrier — a rare combination. Their shared doctrinal advance gave them the capacity for category one love (occupation with Christ), category two love (maximum personal love for each other), and category three impersonal love (doctrine-based love for all believers in their sphere).

4. The marriage of a Jew and a Gentile is presented without qualification as the paradigm of domestic compatibility. Christianity removes the ethnic boundary as a barrier to marriage. What makes the difference in any marriage is not ethnic background but mutual doctrine resident in the soul.

5. The function of ministry requires the team. The noun sunergos — fellow worker — applied to Prisca and Aquila establishes that even the greatest communicator of doctrine depends upon team members. The honor code exists in part to make team function possible.

6. The Royal Family Honor Code is the operational expression of imputed divine righteousness. Half of divine integrity — God's righteousness — has been imputed to every believer at salvation. That righteousness, which is the epitome of divine integrity, demands a system of consistent maintenance: the honor code. Right thinking produces right motivation, which produces right function.

7. Freedom is a four-part system: authority, freedom, privacy, and property. These four elements stand or fall together. To destroy any one of them is to destroy all of them. The privacy of the priesthood is the application of this system to the individual believer's life before God, and it is the foundation of the Royal Family Honor Code.

8. The privacy of the priesthood means live and let live. Every believer has the right to live out his life before the Lord without interference from other believers. The pastor's function is to teach doctrine; the believer's function is to receive it, metabolize it, and apply it. No human authority — pastoral or otherwise — has the right to manage the external life decisions of another believer.

9. Objectivity in doctrine reception requires privacy. The moment a believer becomes conscious of being watched or evaluated by others during the teaching of doctrine, he becomes defensive and loses objectivity. Defensiveness blocks the metabolization of doctrine into epignosis and prevents spiritual growth.

10. Gossip, maligning, and judging are violations of the priesthood of another believer. These are not merely social failings — they are doctrinal offenses that attract divine discipline commensurate with the gravity of the violation. To persist in malicious gossip is to place oneself under the discipline of the justice of God.

Chapter Five Hundred Nineteen

Romans 16:1–4 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Personal and Impersonal Love, Integrity, and Divine Blessing

Romans 16:3–4 “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who laid down their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but also all the churches of the Gentiles.

Romans 16 presents a series of commendations addressed to believers in Rome — men and women of genuine spiritual accomplishment operating within the royal family honor code. The preceding chapter has established the doctrinal substructure; chapter 16 now demonstrates that doctrine applied produces winners: believers who have advanced to maturity and whose lives manifest the integrity of God's plan. The present chapter continues the exposition of the royal family honor code, a theme introduced in connection with verses 1 through 4 and now developed through a series of numbered principles.

I. Personal Love and Impersonal Love: The Foundational Distinction

The royal family honor code commands impersonal love of all believers and personal love of a few. This distinction is not peripheral — it is the axis on which the entire honor code turns.

The Priority of Impersonal Love

Impersonal love must come first. It emphasizes the subject — the norms, standards, character, and integrity of the one who loves. Personal love, by contrast, emphasizes the object — a specific person to whom one is attracted. Because impersonal love is oriented toward the self and its doctrinal content rather than toward the fluctuating qualities of another person, it is the more stable and foundational form of love.

Emotion has no rational capacity, no doctrinal content, and no ability to sustain love through disappointment, conflict, or the full range of human failure. Emotion is an appreciator — it responds to what the mentality of the soul has already processed — but it cannot govern. Personal love, to be valid and durable, requires that emotion be subordinate to the thinking of the soul. This subordination is learned first and most thoroughly in the practice of impersonal love.

Stoic philosophy recognized this principle in part. The Stoics cultivated honor and the subordination of emotion to reason, and in this they achieved something admirable. Their failure was not philosophical but theological: without regeneration, without the ministry of God the Holy Spirit, and without Bible doctrine resident in the soul, the Stoic framework had no content sufficient to sustain it. The shell was present; the reality was absent. Stoicism became a satanic substitute — impressive in form, empty in substance.

The Object and the Subject

Impersonal love is love directed toward all — toward the neighbor (any person in one's periphery, believer or unbeliever) and toward the brethren (fellow members of the royal family of God). In neither case does the quality, behavior, or disposition of the object determine whether love is extended. The standard resides in the subject. The command 'love your neighbor as yourself' and the repeated imperative 'love the brethren' are not commands to personal affection. They are commands to impersonal love — a rational, doctrinal orientation toward others that is entirely independent of emotional attraction or personal compatibility.

Personal love, by contrast, is reserved for a few. It is the love of close friendship, of the right man and right woman relationship, and above all of occupation with the person of the Lord Jesus Christ. One does not arrive at this level of personal love without first having been thoroughly formed by impersonal love. The believer who attempts to manufacture personal affection for everyone in a congregation — straining against genuine antagonism, swallowing genuine irritation, performing a kind of emotional theater — has inverted the order. The result is not love but exhaustion, insincerity, and increased tension.

II. The Honor Code in Practice: Impersonal Love as Aristocratic Function

The royal family of God constitutes a spiritual aristocracy. Every believer at the moment of salvation received the imputation of God's righteousness and was entered into union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. These two realities — imputed divine righteousness and positional union with Christ — form the theological basis of every believer's aristocratic standing. Aristocracy does not perform under the honor code because it feels like it. It performs because the code is the expression of who and what it is.

Concretely, the honor code in a congregation operates as follows: when a fellow believer has maligned, gossiped about, judged, or wronged another, the response governed by the honor code excludes self-defense, counter-attack, retaliatory gossip, and every form of revenge. The matter is left in the Lord's hands. The believer who has been wronged does not lower himself to the level of the one who wronged him. He functions on his own norms and standards — the doctrinal content resident in his conscience and right lobe — and in doing so maintains an infinitely superior position.

This includes the management of privacy. Believers who hold genuine antagonism toward one another are not required to manufacture proximity or simulate warmth. They are required only to respect each other's privacy, to refrain from maligning or judging, and to recognize that God's righteousness has been imputed to the one they dislike just as surely as it has been imputed to themselves. This is the honor code. It does not demand emotional performance. It demands doctrinal integrity.

The honor code also excludes bearing grudges. A grudge is incompatible with impersonal love. When a believer discovers that he is carrying a grudge against another, he knows immediately that he has stepped outside the function of the honor code and must address the condition. Grudges are not resolved by confrontation, emotional catharsis, or enforced reconciliation. They are resolved by rebound — naming the mental attitude sins involved to God — and by the renewed application of doctrinal norms and standards.

The honor code further excludes confusion between flattery and genuine affection. Flattery exploits the emotional register; the believer operating under the honor code is not moved by it. Impersonal love squeezes out the emotional as the governing faculty and restores the mentality of the soul — conscience, right lobe, doctrine — to its proper place of authority.

III. The Theological Basis of Impersonal Love

The command to love the brethren rests on two theological pillars. First, every believer at salvation received the imputation of God's own righteousness. This means that every believer carries within him one half of divine integrity. The other half — divine justice — remains with God and is the channel through which all blessing flows. The presence of imputed righteousness in every believer is not a basis for sentimentality; it is a basis for respect. To practice impersonal love is to respect God's righteousness in another believer even when that believer's behavior is deplorable.

Second, every believer at salvation was entered into union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. This union is the foundation of the royal family of God. Believers are brethren not because they are personally compatible or spiritually equal in their development, but because they share an irreversible positional relationship with the same Lord. The honor code derives from this shared position and is non-negotiable on that basis.

All divine blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God in the believer. This is the central axis of the Epistle to the Romans. Because every believer has imputed righteousness, there is in every believer a target for divine blessing by imputation. The recognition of this fact in another believer is what makes impersonal love possible. You do not love the person on the basis of what he is doing with his life. You love him on the basis of what God has placed in him — righteousness that belongs to God and that forms the basis for God's own engagement with that person's life.

IV. The Relaxed Mental Attitude

A relaxed mental attitude is a component of impersonal love, not of personal love. In personal love, the object of love has the capacity to produce reactions — disappointment, misunderstanding, hurt — that temporarily disrupt mental equilibrium. This is a normal feature of intimate personal relationship. In impersonal love, however, a relaxed mental attitude is not optional. It is the expression of doctrinal stability applied to relationships across the entire congregation.

A non-relaxed mental attitude in the domain of impersonal love involves mental attitude sins: arrogance, jealousy, hatred, antagonism, bitterness, implacability, vindictiveness, and guilt reaction. These sins disqualify the believer from functioning under the honor code and from advancing toward maturity. They are to be named to God and abandoned, not managed through emotional suppression or religious performance.

The filling of the Holy Spirit is the prerequisite for the relaxed mental attitude. Without the filling of the Spirit and maximum doctrine in the soul, the honor code cannot be sustained. The believer who attempts to manufacture the relaxed mental attitude through willpower or social convention will fail. The source is always spiritual: the Spirit filling the believer who has named known sins to God and is internalizing the word.

V. Point Four — The Common Objective of the Honor Code

Point four of the royal family honor code: the honor code recognizes the common objective for every believer in time.

No honor code can be sustained without a clear and shared objective. Military academy honor codes exist to instill personal integrity and self-governance in officer candidates. Medieval honor codes were designed in many cases to protect the dignity of womanhood and to transmit that value across generations. Every honor code, whatever its quality, is organized around stated objectives.

The common objective of the royal family honor code is spiritual advance. This advance follows a three-stage trajectory. In the first stage — from new birth through the early phases of Christian life — the believer is supported by the laws of divine establishment and begins accumulating doctrinal content under the ministry of a communicator. In the second stage, the believer moves toward the maturity barrier, sustained by logistical grace and the consistent perception of doctrine. In the third stage, having cracked the maturity barrier, the believer advances through supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace, functioning at maximum capacity within the honor code.

At every point, the honor code serves this objective by creating the conditions under which doctrine can be received without distraction. When believers respect each other's privacy, refrain from mental attitude sins, and function on their own norms and standards rather than reacting to the failures of others, the local church becomes an environment conducive to advance. The honor code is not an end in itself; it is an operational framework in service of the advance to maturity.

The advance is accomplished through delegated authority operating in two directions: the canon of Scripture and the communication of doctrine through the spiritual gift of pastor-teacher. These two channels are inseparable in practice. The canon specifies the mechanism of recovery from sin — rebound, the naming of known sins to God in accordance with 1 John 1:9 — and every addition to that mechanism, whether emotional, penitential, or sacrificial, constitutes a rejection of scriptural authority. The believer who insists on feeling guilty, confessing to others, promising God he will never sin again, or performing some compensatory act has substituted emotional authority for canonical authority and cannot advance.

VI. Point Five — The Honor Code Builds Integrity Without Rejecting Morality

Point five: the honor code builds integrity but does not reject morality.

A common misapplication of the honor code is the inference that, because the Christian standard exceeds mere morality, morality itself is dispensable. This is antinomianism — a distortion of grace. Morality is designed for the entire human race: believers and unbelievers alike. It is the expression of the laws of divine establishment applied to human conduct. An unbeliever can be moral without being a Christian; morality does not produce salvation. But the existence of morality as a lower standard does not give the believer license to operate below it.

The integrity that the honor code builds operates at a level above morality. Its source is the filling of the Holy Spirit combined with maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Christianity exceeds morality; it does not exclude it. In the same way that Christians affirm freedom — a principle that belongs to the entire human race under divine establishment — without imagining that their affirmation of freedom is unique to Christianity, so Christians affirm morality without imagining that their integrity is reducible to it.

VII. Point Six — The Honor Code Excludes Production as a Means of Blessing

Point six: the honor code excludes Christian production as the means of blessing from God.

Every believer wears two hats. The first is the royal priesthood: the believer stands before God as a priest, advancing from salvation to maturity through the reception and internalization of Bible doctrine. The second is the royal ambassadorship: the believer functions in the world as a representative of the Lord Jesus Christ, producing — through prayer, witnessing, giving, teaching, and other works — in accordance with his spiritual gift and level of maturity.

The priesthood is the basis of blessing from God. The ambassadorship produces works. These two must not be confused. Tithing does not produce blessing. Witnessing does not produce blessing. Serving in ministry does not produce blessing. Prayer for others, however sincere and however fruitful for those prayed for, does not produce the believer's own blessing from God. God blesses the believer because the believer has capacity for blessing — capacity that is the product of maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

Blessing by divine imputation flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God in the mature believer. This is the adjustment to the justice of God at the maturity level. God is glorified in blessing the believer who has maximum doctrine. It is not that God rewards activity; it is that God imputes blessing to the target that His own righteousness has established in the believer's soul. The attainment of maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul is the one and only means by which blessing is received as a real imputation.

This does not mean that immature believers receive no provision from God. Logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued advance — sustains every believer from the moment of salvation. But logistical grace is not the same as the mature blessing that comes with the cracking of the maturity barrier. And blessing by association — the overflow of blessing from a mature believer to those in his periphery — accounts for much of what appears to be prosperity in the lives of believers who have not yet advanced to maturity.

VIII. Point Seven — Total Dependence on the Integrity of God: Hope

Point seven: total dependence on the integrity of God is called hope.

Biblical hope is not wishful thinking or emotional optimism. Hope, in the technical theological sense, is confident expectation — the certain anticipation of a promised blessing that has not yet been received but is guaranteed by the integrity of God.

Three categories of hope correspond to the three stages of spiritual advance. The first hope is the confident anticipation of salvation: the prospect of eternal life that motivates and enables the act of faith in Christ. Once faith is exercised, the hope gives way to the reality of salvation adjustment, and the hope is set aside.

The second hope is the confident anticipation of mature blessing — the certain expectation that consistent doctrine intake will result in the cracking of the maturity barrier and the reception of supergrace blessings. This hope functions as the motivator that keeps the believer pressing forward through the long middle of the Christian life, when progress may be invisible and resistance may be intense. When the maturity barrier is cracked, the reality displaces the hope.

The third hope is the confident anticipation of eschatological reward — the certain expectation of blessing, reward, and glorification that will be imputed to the mature believer at the judgment seat of Christ following the rapture. The mature believer carries this hope as an absolute confidence throughout his life, and it becomes the deepest and most permanent motivator for continued function under the honor code.

Hope in each of its three categories is the operational expression of total dependence on the integrity of God. The believer does not depend on his own performance, his production, his emotion, or any human system. He depends on the justice of God, which is committed by its own character to bless the righteousness of God wherever it resides in a mature believer. This dependence is the ultimate form of the honor code.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Nineteen

1. Impersonal love precedes and grounds personal love. The command to love all believers — the neighbor and the brethren — is a command to impersonal love, not personal affection. Impersonal love emphasizes the subject's norms and standards; personal love emphasizes the object. The believer who has not first developed impersonal love through doctrinal formation is not ready for the deeper commitments of personal love.

2. Emotion is an appreciator, not a governor. Emotion has no doctrinal content and no rational capacity. It must be subordinate to the mentality of the soul. The Christian way of life does not suppress emotion, but it does not allow emotion to function as the criterion for spiritual evaluation or as the basis for love. How one feels is never the issue; what one thinks — what doctrine resides in the right lobe — is always the issue.

3. The theological basis of impersonal love is the imputation of divine righteousness to every believer. Because God's righteousness has been credited to every believer at salvation, every believer carries within him a permanent theological dignity that demands respect. Impersonal love is the practical recognition of this reality. It does not require approval of another believer's conduct; it requires respect for what God has placed in him.

4. A relaxed mental attitude is required for impersonal love. Mental attitude sins — arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, implacability, hatred — are incompatible with impersonal love and with the honor code. They must be addressed through rebound and replaced by the doctrinal norms and standards resident in the soul. The filling of the Holy Spirit is the indispensable prerequisite.

5. Grudges are incompatible with the honor code. A believer who discovers he is carrying a grudge knows immediately that he has stepped outside the function of the royal family honor code. Grudges are not managed — they are relinquished through rebound and the renewed application of doctrinal standards.

6. The common objective of the honor code is spiritual advance. The honor code exists not as an end in itself but as the operational framework within which doctrine is received, maturity is achieved, and the local church functions as an environment conducive to the advance of every believer. All authority in the church — canonical and pastoral — is in service of this objective.

7. The honor code builds integrity but does not reject morality. Christianity exceeds the standard of morality without abandoning it. The integrity that the honor code produces is sourced in the filling of the Spirit and maximum doctrine; it operates at a level above what morality can achieve or require. The antinomian inference — that grace releases the believer from moral obligation — is a distortion.

8. Production is not the means of blessing; maturity is. The royal ambassadorship produces works; the royal priesthood is the basis of blessing by imputation. No amount of service, giving, prayer, witnessing, or ministry activity produces blessing from God. God blesses the mature believer because the mature believer has capacity — maximum doctrine resident in the soul — which constitutes the target for divine imputation of blessing.

9. Hope is the motivational expression of total dependence on the integrity of God. The three categories of hope — anticipation of salvation, anticipation of mature blessing, and anticipation of eschatological reward — correspond to the three stages of spiritual advance and function as the motivators that sustain the believer's momentum under the honor code. Hope is not emotion; it is certain expectation based on the character of God.
