Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two

Romans 16:5 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Personal and Impersonal Love, Morality and Integrity, Hope, Production, and the Dying Phase of Living

Romans 16:3–4 “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Greet Priska and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.

Romans 16:5 resumes the verse-by-verse exposition, but the immediate context is the continuing reorganization of the doctrine of the Royal Family Honor Code. This chapter addresses the final ten points of that doctrine — moving through impersonal love, morality and integrity, hope as motivation, the place of production, logistical grace, self-pity, self-righteousness, and the honor code's application even in the dying phase of living.

I. Point Six of the Honor Code: Personal Love and Impersonal Love

The command to love the brethren cannot be fulfilled until the believer understands the difference between the essential and the non-essential, and the difference between personal love and impersonal love. These two categories are not interchangeable; conflating them produces either hypocrisy or spiritual breakdown.

A. Defining the Two Categories

Impersonal love emphasizes the subject — the believer's own norms, standards, and mental attitude — and directs itself toward all persons within the believer's periphery. Personal love emphasizes the object and is directed toward only a few persons.

Three categories of personal love may be distinguished: (1) category one, directed toward the Lord Jesus Christ; (2) category two, directed toward right man or right woman; and (3) category three, directed toward a circle of close friends. Personal love assigns merit to the object and involves attraction, mutual interest, and emotional response. Impersonal love assigns no merit to the object whatsoever — its integrity derives entirely from the norms and standards residing in the subject.

B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code

The following sub-points define the structure and function of impersonal love as a component of the Royal Family Honor Code.

1. The command to love the brethren can never be fulfilled until the believer understands the difference between the essential and the non-essential, and between personal and impersonal love.

2. Impersonal love emphasizes the subject; personal love emphasizes the object.

3. Impersonal love depends on the norms and standards of the subject.

4. Impersonal love directs itself toward all persons within the believer's periphery — both fellow believers (cf. John 15:12, 17; 1 John 3:23) and neighbors in the broader sense (cf. Romans 13:8–9; 1 Peter 2:17; 3:8).

5. Personal love is directed toward a few; impersonal love is directed toward all.

6. The object of impersonal love is all believers and everyone within the believer's periphery.

7. Impersonal love excludes emotion. Personal love has great emotional function, because emotion serves as an appreciator — it responds to what is valued. But when dealing with the human race in general, the subject's norms and standards govern, and emotion is excluded from the operational dynamic.

8. Impersonal love emphasizes the integrity of the subject; personal love emphasizes the attractiveness of the object.

9. Impersonal love cannot be reduced to the level of dog-eat-dog. When another person gossips, maligns, competes, or acts out of jealousy or vindictiveness, impersonal love prevents the believer from descending to that person's broken standards. To operate on the antagonist's standards is to share in their weakness rather than allowing them to benefit from the believer's strength.

10. Impersonal love therefore excludes carrying a grudge.

11. If wronged, the believer under impersonal love does not seek revenge. Retaliation would lower the believer to the standards of the antagonist.

12. Impersonal love includes respect for the imputed righteousness of God residing in every other believer.

13. Since the righteousness of God — one half of divine integrity — resides in every believer, impersonal love respects the other believer on that basis alone.

14. The believer cannot hold a grudge against another believer. To do so is equivalent to bearing a grudge against the righteousness of God — which is blasphemous.

15. Impersonal love is the relaxed mental attitude produced by the filling of the Spirit (Romans 5:5; Galatians 5:22), not overt friendliness or effusive hypocrisy. When Romans 5:5 and Galatians 5:22 speak of the Spirit producing love, the reference is to impersonal love, not personal love.

16. Under impersonal love, the believer functions under his own doctrinal norms and standards rather than being influenced by flattery, attraction, attention, or reciprocity.

17. Impersonal love not only excludes mental and verbal sins, but demands toleration, respect for privacy, and the avoidance of distracting others from doctrine.

18. Flexibility is related to impersonal love.

19. Personal love, by contrast, emphasizes the object and demands learning to know that object — whether Christ, right man or right woman, or close friends. It demands genuine cognizance of the person involved.

Key passages for review in connection with this point: Romans 12:9; Romans 13:8–10.

II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code

The seventh major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code concerns the relationship between morality and the Christian way of life.

1. Morality is designed for the fulfillment of the laws of divine establishment and is therefore designed for the entire human race, believers included.

2. Since the unbeliever can produce morality, morality is not in itself a component of the Christian way of life.

3. While the Christian way of life is not morality, it does not exclude morality. The Christian way of life is higher than morality.

4. The honor code demands a standard superior to morality for the royal family of God.

5. Christianity uses the morality of divine establishment as a base, but exceeds that base in the function of the honor code. Morality does not demand impersonal love; impersonal love is a higher standard than morality.

6. Anything the unbeliever can do is not the Christian way of life. The Christian way of life is a supernatural way of life, which demands a supernatural means of execution — namely, the filling of the Holy Spirit. The unbeliever can fulfill morality without the Spirit. The filling of the Spirit is required to function under impersonal love. Hell is filled with moral people — the rich young ruler being the paradigm case: perfectly moral, yet an unbeliever (cf. Mark 10:17–22).

7. Morality is not rejected as per antinomianism, nor is morality elevated to a saving or sanctifying mechanism as per legalism.

8. Neither legalism nor antinomianism is the Christian way of life.

9. The honor code demands that the believer live under establishment but exceed the morality of establishment through the perception of doctrine and the filling of the Holy Spirit.

10. Both the morality of establishment and the integrity of the honor code support the believer's advance toward the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

11. The honor code demands patriotism, respect for governmental authority, military service, and respect for law and order in the believer's relationship with the civil government (cf. Romans 13:1–7).

Passage for review: Romans 13:1–7.

III. Point Eight: Hope as Motivation and Momentum in the Honor Code

Hope, defined as confident anticipation or confident expectation regarding the future, functions as both the motivation and the momentum in the believer's advance through the Protocol Plan of God. It is not wishful thinking but a category of certain expectation grounded in divine promises.

Hope operates not only as the motivator in the advance toward maturity but as the motivator in the function of Christian integrity. The doctrine of hope, already treated in detail in prior chapters, bears directly on the honor code. Romans 15:13–14 specifically connects hope to the function of the honor code and should be reviewed in this connection.

IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code

The ninth major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code is the principle of production and its proper relationship to the priesthood and ambassadorship of every believer.

1. A distinction must be maintained between the believer's royal priesthood and royal ambassadorship. Every believer holds both offices from the moment of salvation.

2. As a royal priest, the believer advances through persistent perception of doctrine.

3. As a royal ambassador, the believer produces as a result of spiritual growth — never as the means of spiritual growth. No legitimate production can exist apart from the ministry of the Spirit.

4. The Royal Family Honor Code excludes all forms of Christian works — whether legitimate or illegitimate — as a means of blessing from God.

5. Nothing accomplished in the areas of witnessing, praying, giving, worshiping, sacrificing, or church service can bring divine blessing as an earned reward.

6. Neither morality, talent, personality change, asceticism, sacrificial giving, devotional worship, nor church work will elicit blessing from God as its cause.

7. Blessing from God originates from doctrine resident in the soul, which produces capacity for life, which in turn triggers the imputation of divine blessing to the target — the imputed righteousness of God residing in the mature believer.

8. Divine blessing is a real imputation from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God — the home address of divine blessing in the believer at the point of maturity.

9. The attainment of maturity through maximum doctrine perceived is the only basis for the imputation of divine blessing. The advance from salvation to maturity, through the filling of the Spirit and doctrine in the soul, produces Christian production. But production is always the result of blessing, never its means. The means of blessing from God is in the priesthood; the result is expressed in ambassadorship.

10. What is often construed as blessing from God is either logistical grace or blessing by association.

A. Logistical Grace

Under logistical grace, God provides every support necessary for the believer to attain maturity. This support is individualized — no two believers receive the same allocation. The components include:

— Time: No two believers are given the same span of life.

— Food, shelter, clothing: All variable in kind and quantity.

— Transportation: The means by which the believer reaches the local assembly for doctrine intake — whatever that means may be.

— Financial provision: The believer's effective 'allowance' from God, determined by divine wisdom regarding what the believer can be trusted to handle.

— A right pastor-teacher and a local church: The assembly through which doctrine is communicated.

The variation in logistical support is not an index of spiritual status. The Apostle Paul died without material wealth and yet is the greatest believer of the Church Age. Philippians 4:11–12 records his statement: 'I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound.' The honor code prohibits self-pity and envy arising from comparison of one believer's logistical support with another's.

B. Blessing by Association

Under blessing by association, a believer may receive material and providential blessing from God not because of his own maturity but because he is associated with a mature believer — a family member, colleague, or friend through whom the mature believer's imputed blessing overflows. This explains the apparent prosperity of some believers who have not yet attained maturity.

13. The Royal Family Honor Code demands total dependence on the integrity of God rather than dependence on one's own ability or human achievement. This is not an excuse to cease productive effort; rather, the believer is motivated to work hard while understanding that the ultimate source of every provision is divine integrity.

14. The purpose of the honor code is to provide the necessary privacy, protection from bullying, and survival in life during the advance to maturity.

15. Works are the result of the advance, never the means of advance in Christianity. Production may be a manifestation of spiritual progress, but it is never the means of spiritual progress.

V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer

The Royal Family Honor Code demands more of the strong or mature believer than of the weak. Romans 15:1 states: 'Now we, the strong, are obligated under the honor code to keep bearing the weaknesses of the weak and not to accommodate ourselves.' As the believer advances toward maturity, he not only carries his own weight but assumes the burden of tolerating those who are ignorant of doctrine.

Bearing the weaknesses of the weak is the maximum utilization of impersonal love and total toleration in the area of the non-essentials. The strong believer who operates under maximum doctrine and the filling of the Spirit is able to tolerate the erroneous and inconsequential opinions formulated from ignorance, without being drawn down to that level. This is strength through flexibility.

The weak believer is weak because he has little understanding of doctrine and formulates inconsequential opinions about superficialities of life with maximum arrogance. The mature believer's function of impersonal love fulfills his honor code duty to the weak believer, placing all emphasis on his own doctrinal norms and standards rather than on the merit or demerit of the weak believer as an object.

Passage for review: Romans 15:1–4.

VI. Point Eleven: Authority Orientation and Momentum

The thrust of the honor code demands authority orientation as the basis for continued momentum in the Christian way of life. This encompasses the full structure of divinely ordained authority in the spiritual realm — pastor-teacher, local assembly, the canon of Scripture — and will be developed in subsequent treatment.

VII. Point Twelve: Reciprocity in the Honor Code

Reciprocity is a component of the honor code. The principle is found in Romans 15:26–27, where the Gentile churches' contribution to the Jerusalem saints is framed as the discharge of a spiritual debt — those who have received spiritual benefit are obligated to minister to those who provided it in material terms. This reciprocity is not legalism but honor-code obligation arising from genuine gratitude and impersonal love.

VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity

The Royal Family Honor Code demands the avoidance of self-pity and of any behavior designed to arouse pity from others. Self-pity is among the most powerful distractions from the spiritual life, because it directs the believer's attention inward and away from doctrine.

When another person takes an interest in a believer because they feel sorry for him, that interest is not genuine friendship but compassion. A relationship built on manufactured sympathy severs the believer from reality and produces a pattern of behavior — deliberate exhibition of vulnerability to elicit attention — that is incompatible with the honor code.

Romans 12:9 states that love must be non-hypocritical. Impersonal love is free from hypocrisy because it operates on the subject's own norms and standards, not on a calculated performance for the benefit of an observer. Romans 12:9–10 and 13:8 demand a response of impersonal love, not personal love, toward the general body of believers. Attempting to fulfill these impersonal-love commands through personal love will produce either spiritual breakdown or hypocrisy.

Since impersonal love depends upon doctrinal standards resident in the conscience, it excludes self-pity on the part of the subject and repudiates any operational pattern designed to arouse pity in others.

Passages for review: Romans 12:9–10; 13:8; 14:8; 15:5–7.

IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness

The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation eliminates the function of self-righteousness in the Christian way of life. The Royal Family Honor Code therefore excludes self-righteousness entirely.

1. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness, never self-righteousness. The self-righteous believer who presents his moral achievements to God as grounds for blessing misunderstands the nature of divine integrity.

2. Self-righteousness functions in all three categories of the old sin nature's modus operandi. It produces arrogance, human good, and evil — including the ideological evil of statism and collectivism.

3. Self-righteousness is a complex of evil eliminated by the function of the honor code.

4. Self-righteousness plus sincerity guarantees the function of evil in the believer's life.

5. Self-righteousness is not only excluded from the honor code, but its very presence in the believer's life constitutes an insult to the integrity and holiness of God and a blasphemous denial of the divine provision of logistical grace.

X. Point Fifteen: The Maximum Function of the Honor Code — Risking Life for Another

The maximum expression of the Royal Family Honor Code is to risk or give one's life for another member of the royal family. Romans 16:3–4 presents this in concrete historical terms: Priska and Aquila 'risked their own necks' for the Apostle Paul, and all the Gentile churches joined Paul in giving thanks for their sacrifice.

This principle is grounded in the Lord Jesus Christ's own statement in John 15:12–13: 'This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.' See also Romans 5:7 and 1 John 3:16.

XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living

The final major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code addresses the dying phase of living. In human thinking, dying is categorized as the cessation of living. The honor code, however, refuses that equation: as long as the believer draws breath, the Christian way of life is fully operative.

A terminal diagnosis, confinement to a hospital bed, and isolation from the normal activities of life do not suspend the honor code. The dying phase of living is not the absence of life but one of its most demanding arenas. For the believer with maximum doctrine resident in the soul, the dying phase becomes the greatest challenge and the greatest opportunity for the application of that doctrine.

Philippians 1:20–21 captures the principle: 'According to my intense concentration on doctrine and resultant hope, that in nothing shall I be disgraced, but with integrity of the honor code, even now as always, Christ shall be exalted in my person, whether by living or by dying. For me, living is Christ and dying is gain.' The honor code therefore makes greater demands in the dying phase of living than in any living phase, because it requires that doctrine be applied under maximum pressure and minimum external support — a condition that only maximum doctrine in the soul and the filling of the Spirit can sustain.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two

1. Impersonal love and personal love are structurally distinct. Impersonal love is governed by the subject's norms and standards and directed toward all persons. Personal love is governed by attraction to a specific object and directed toward only a few. Collapsing these two categories produces either hypocrisy or psychological breakdown.

2. The filling of the Holy Spirit produces impersonal love, not personal love. Romans 5:5 and Galatians 5:22 refer to the Spirit's production of impersonal love as a relaxed mental attitude — not to an emotion directed toward a specific person. The filling of the Spirit is required for impersonal love; it is not required for mere morality.

3. Morality is not the Christian way of life but its foundation. Since the unbeliever can produce morality without the filling of the Spirit, morality is not a component unique to Christianity. The Christian way of life exceeds morality through the function of the honor code under the Spirit's control. The honor code is neither legalism nor antinomianism.

4. Production is always the result of advance, never its means. All blessing flows from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God residing in the mature believer. Works, witnessing, giving, and moral achievement cannot produce divine blessing as their cause. Logistical grace supports the advance to maturity; blessing by association may benefit those not yet mature.

5. Logistical grace is individualized. God provides precisely the resources — time, food, shelter, transportation, financial provision, and a right pastor-teacher — that each believer requires for the advance to maturity. Variation in logistical support is not an index of spiritual status. Self-pity arising from comparison with others violates the honor code.

6. The mature believer bears the burdens of the weak. Romans 15:1 assigns to the strong the obligation to bear the weaknesses of the weak rather than accommodating themselves. This is maximum impersonal love in function — tolerance of the inconsequential opinions of doctrinally weak believers, executed through doctrinal norms and the filling of the Spirit, not through emotional forbearance.

7. Self-pity is incompatible with the honor code. Impersonal love operates on the subject's own standards and assigns no merit to the object. It therefore excludes self-pity and any operational pattern designed to elicit pity from others. Relationships built on manufactured sympathy are incompatible with genuine honor-code function.

8. Imputed righteousness eliminates self-righteousness. Divine justice blesses divine righteousness, not self-righteousness. Self-righteousness — a complex of arrogance, human good, and evil — is excluded by the honor code and constitutes an insult to divine integrity and a denial of logistical grace.

9. Dying is a phase of living under the honor code. Philippians 1:20–21 establishes that Christ is exalted whether by living or by dying. The honor code remains fully operative in the terminal phase of physical life and makes greater demands there than in any other phase, because the application of maximum doctrine under maximum pressure is the highest expression of the Christian way of life.

10. The maximum expression of the honor code is self-sacrifice for a fellow believer. Romans 16:3–4, John 15:12–13, Romans 5:7, and 1 John 3:16 converge on the principle that the willingness to risk or give one's life for another member of the royal family is the apex of honor-code function.

Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three

Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia

Romans 16:5 “Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Also pay my respects to the church in their home. Greet Epinetus, my beloved friend, who is the first convert to Christ from Asia — the Roman province of Asia.

Romans 16 continues the honor roll of mature believers who assembled in the homes of Priska and Aquila and in two other house-churches in Rome. The chapter exhibits the royal family honor code — the operational standard of conduct for Church Age believers — as it was lived out by identifiable historical persons. Verses 1 through 4 introduced Phoebe, a mature single woman who served the church at Cenchreae, and the married couple Priska and Aquila, who risked their lives for Paul and hosted a local church in their home. Verse 5 introduces Epinetus, the first convert to Christ from the Roman province of Asia. The present chapter examines point sixteen of the royal family honor code — that dying is a part of living — and then turns to the grammatical and theological analysis of verse 5.

I. Point Sixteen of the Royal Family Honor Code: Dying as a Part of Living

The royal family honor code culminates in a principle without parallel in any human ethical system: dying is not assigned to the category of death but to the category of life. The dying phase of physical existence is as much a part of living as any other dimension of life. This principle is grounded in the dynamics of Bible doctrine resident in the soul and reaches its ultimate expression in Philippians 1:20–21.

A. The Anatomy of Physical Death

Every human body is a temporary dwelling — a tent — that houses both the human soul and, for the believer, the human spirit. Human life was imputed to the soul at physical birth; eternal life was imputed to the human spirit at regeneration. The believer therefore carries two categories of life simultaneously within a mortal frame. At physical death, soul and spirit depart from the body and the believer is immediately face to face with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The departure itself is not the problem. The problem is the dying — the days, weeks, or months of deterioration, pain, isolation, or sudden violence that precede the moment of departure.

Dying is always a solitary act. No companion can share the experience. A person may enjoy a symphony, a meal, or a conversation with another; no one can die alongside another in the sense of bearing that death for him. Physical death is the one test in human existence that must be faced and executed entirely alone. This is the reason it constitutes the supreme test of the Christian life: it is the one arena where only the doctrine resident in the believer's own soul is available as a resource.

B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying

The mature believer who has accumulated maximum doctrine in the soul — through the consistent daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) — carries that doctrine directly into the dying phase without interruption. Capacity for life in living, built on maximum doctrine resident in the soul, translates without diminution into capacity for life in dying. The dynamics are identical: right thinking produces right motivation; right motivation produces right action. This sequence operates in the dying phase precisely as it operates in the living phase.

Logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence — does not terminate at the onset of terminal illness or mortal danger. The same Lord, the same logistical support, the same indwelling Spirit, and the same doctrine are present in dying as in living. God has no intention of withdrawing His support from the positive believer at the moment of his greatest test.

Undeserved suffering, when handled with doctrine and without self-pity, functions as preparation for dying. The believer who can handle undeserved suffering with occupation with Christ and stability of soul has already demonstrated the inner resources that will carry him through the dying phase. The believer who panics at undeserved suffering has revealed that those inner resources are not yet in place.

C. The Contrast with the Unbeliever

For the unbeliever, dying typically represents the nadir of existence. Without eternal life imputed to a human spirit, without Bible doctrine in the soul, and without the indwelling Holy Spirit, the unbeliever faces dying with no inner resources. Beyond death lies the appointment with judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The unbeliever may achieve a degree of poise or dignity through the resources of human character — as certain historical figures have demonstrated at the point of execution — but these resources, however admirable, are of a different order entirely from the occupation with Christ that sustains the mature believer.

D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace

The theological framework that supports the dying-as-living principle is the three-hope schema developed earlier in the epistle. The first hope rests on the imputation of human life at birth and the judicial imputation of Adam's sin, which establishes the need for salvation. The gospel addresses that need, and faith in Christ replaces the hope with the reality of eternal salvation — the first adjustment to the justice of God.

The second hope rests on the two judicial imputations at the cross: all personal sins imputed to Christ and judged, and the righteousness of God imputed to the believer at salvation. This produces the second potential — the blessing of time, including dying grace as its ultimate expression. Consistent perception of doctrine advances the believer toward cracking the maturity barrier. The reality that replaces the second hope is the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

The third hope rests on the imputation of eternal life to the human spirit at regeneration and on the blessings imputed at maturity, with dying grace as the final and greatest of those blessings. Undeserved suffering, handled with doctrine, functions as a rehearsal for the dying phase and contributes to the third hope — absolute confidence regarding the eternal future: the resurrection body, the judgment seat of Christ, the imputation of eternal reward and blessing, and the eternal state in which there is no more death, sorrow, tears, or pain.

E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code

The scriptural anchor for point sixteen is Philippians 1:20–21. Paul writes from the vantage point of a believer who has advanced to ultra-supergrace and who faces the real possibility of execution. The passage reads:

Philippians 1:20–21 “as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: According to my intense concentration on doctrine and resultant hope that in nothing shall I be disgraced, but with the integrity of the honor code, even now as always, Christ shall be exalted in my person, whether by life or by death. For me, living is Christ; and dying — which is still a part of living — is gain.

The phrase 'whether by life or by death' eliminates any categorical distinction between living and dying as spheres of Christian function. Both are arenas for the exaltation of Christ. The declaration 'living is Christ' marks the condition of maximum doctrine resident in the soul — occupation with the person of Christ as the organizing center of all thought and motivation. When living is Christ, dying is not loss but gain — profit — because the same occupation with Christ that generates capacity in living generates greater capacity in dying. Dying becomes the highest expression of the honor code, not the negation of it.

The honor code is the only ethical system that assigns dying to the category of life and makes it the ultimate achievement of Christian existence. The mature believer does not have two modes — a living mode and a dying mode — because occupation with Christ is a continuous state that admits no interruption. The unbeliever and the immature believer are compelled to change modes; the mature believer is not.

II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila

Verse 5 opens with a continuation of Paul's greetings to the believers assembled in Rome. The first clause directs attention to the local church that met in the private residence of Priska and Aquila.

The conjunction kai (καί) functions here in its adjunctive sense: also. The corrected translation therefore begins: Also pay my respects to the church in their home. No verb for 'greet' appears explicitly in the Greek; the aorist active imperative of aspázomai (ἀσπάζομαι) is implied from the surrounding context. Aspázomai means to greet, to salute, to pay one's respects to a person of honor.

The local church is identified by the accusative singular of ekklēsía (ἐκκλησία), the standard term for the local assembly. The phrase kata plus oíkos (κατά + οἶκος) — prepositional phrase governing the genitive plural of the intensive pronoun autós used as a possessive — specifies the location: in their home. The genitive plural indicates that the home belongs jointly to Priska and Aquila.

The practice of assembling for church services in private residences was characteristic of the first century of the Church Age. Comparable references appear in Acts 12:17, 1 Corinthians 16:19, Colossians 4:15, and Philemon 2. The home of Priska and Aquila was large enough to serve as one of at least three such assembly points mentioned in Romans 16. The identity of the pastor of this particular congregation is not specified; it is possible that Aquila himself served in that capacity, given his demonstrated spiritual maturity.

III. Romans 16:5b — Epinetus: The First Convert from Asia

A. Grammatical Analysis

The verse continues with the aorist active imperative of aspázomai (ἀσπάζομαι), here expressed explicitly. The aorist is a constantive aorist — it contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety and refers to a momentary, complete act: the uttering of a word of greeting or the gesture of a salute. The active voice indicates that Paul himself produces the action; the imperative mood is the imperative of entreaty, conveying a request rather than a command. Paul is asking the Roman believers to extend his personal respects to Epinetus.

The accusative singular direct object is the proper noun Epínetos (Ἐπαίνετος). This is an uncommon name; an inscription discovered in Rome records an individual named Epinetus the Ephesian, and the identification with the person named here is well supported.

Paul qualifies Epinetus with the accusative singular adjective agapētós (ἀγαπητός), meaning beloved — one who is the object of deep personal affection. The possessive genitive singular of egó (ἐγώ) — my — specifies that this is Paul's own expression of personal love. Epinetus is not merely the recipient of Paul's impersonal love for the brethren generally; he is Paul's beloved friend, the object of category-three personal love.

The relative clause that follows employs the nominative singular relative pronoun hós (ὅς), whose antecedent is Epinetus. With this is the present active indicative of eimí (εἰμί), the verb of being, functioning here as a historical present — a past event described with the vividness of a present occurrence. The predicate nominative is aparchḗ (ἀπαρχή), meaning first fruits or first convert.

The ablative of source governs the proper noun Asia (Ἀσία). The King James renders this 'Achaia,' but the best manuscripts read Asia — the Roman proconsular province of Asia, located in western Asia Minor (modern western Turkey). This province included the seven churches addressed in Revelation 2–3 and encompassed the sub-regions of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia. Ephesus was the administrative capital. The phrase eis Christón (εἰς Χριστόν) — to Christ — completes the clause.

Corrected translation of Romans 16:5b: Greet Epinetus, my beloved friend, who is the first convert to Christ from Asia — the Roman province of Asia.

B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus

Epinetus was almost certainly the first person Paul led to faith in Christ during his ministry in Ephesus, the principal city of the Roman province of Asia. He subsequently relocated to Rome. By the time of Paul's letter, he had continued positive toward Bible doctrine, had advanced to spiritual maturity, and had become one of the recognized leaders in the house-church of Priska and Aquila. He represents what may be called the non-spectacular type of mature believer.

Epinetus is not identified in the New Testament with any dramatic act, apostolic mission, or visible leadership role beyond what can be inferred from his presence on this honor roll. He is not a rocket — he is a horse. His advance to maturity was not accomplished through any single spectacular burst of spiritual energy but through the slow, steady, continuous intake of Bible doctrine over many years: plugging, persevering, maintaining positive volition regardless of setbacks, ostracism, failure, or the disappearance of encouraging companions.

Even after Paul's direct ministry was no longer available to him, Epinetus continued to take in doctrine — possibly under the teaching of Aquila in Rome. He was consistent in his attendance at the assembly in the home of Priska and Aquila. He was diligent in concentration on the teaching of doctrine, making the function of GAP a daily habit. Self-determination and positive volition toward doctrine, maintained day by day, were the operative factors in his advance.

The result was capacity for life in all its dimensions: capacity in living, and — according to the logic of point sixteen — greater capacity in dying. Epinetus had, through sustained doctrine intake, accumulated the inner resources that no external circumstance can supply and no external pressure can take away. He lived an honorable life that glorified the Lord Jesus Christ, and he died an honorable death that glorified the Lord Jesus Christ.

Epinetus therefore stands as a fulfillment of Philippians 1:20–21. He is the ordinary believer who achieved the extraordinary through the one mechanism available to every member of the royal family of God: consistent, daily, positive volition toward the Word of God.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three

1. Point sixteen of the royal family honor code: The honor code is the only ethical system that assigns dying to the category of life. Dying is as much a part of living as any other dimension of human existence for the Church Age believer. This principle has no parallel in secular ethics and cannot be grasped apart from Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

2. Physical death is a solitary act: No companion, friend, or fellow believer can share the dying experience. Every believer must face and execute his own dying. This makes dying the supreme test of the Christian life, because it is the one arena where only the doctrine in the believer's own soul is available as a resource. The quality of that dying is a direct measure of the doctrine accumulated over a lifetime.

3. Logistical grace does not terminate at the onset of dying: The same Lord, the same provision, the same indwelling Spirit, and the same Bible doctrine that sustained the believer in living are present in dying. God does not withdraw His support at the moment of the greatest test. The positive believer can therefore face dying with the same inner resources available in every prior circumstance of life.

4. Undeserved suffering is preparation for dying: The believer who handles undeserved suffering with doctrine, without self-pity or bitterness, has demonstrated the inner resources that will sustain him through the dying phase. Conversely, the believer who is still shocked by what people do, or who collapses under undeserved suffering, has revealed that his doctrine intake has not yet produced the stability required for dying grace.

5. The three-hope schema culminates in dying grace: The second hope includes the imputation of divine blessing in time, with dying grace as its ultimate expression. The third hope encompasses the full range of eternal blessing — resurrection body, judgment seat of Christ, eternal reward — beginning from the point of maturity. Dying grace is therefore the apex of time-blessing and the threshold of eternity.

6. Philippians 1:20–21 is the definitive statement of the honor code's ultimate: Intense concentration on doctrine produces the resultant hope that the believer will not be disgraced in dying. When living is Christ — when occupation with the person of Christ is the organizing center of the believer's inner life — dying is gain. The exaltation of Christ occurs in both spheres without distinction. There is no mode-shift for the mature believer.

7. The kai in Romans 16:5a is adjunctive: The conjunction should be rendered 'also' rather than 'likewise.' The implied verb is the aorist active imperative of aspázomai — to greet, to salute, to pay one's respects. The local church assembling in the home of Priska and Aquila in Rome is one of at least three house-churches identified in Romans 16.

8. The Roman province of Asia, not Achaia, is the correct reading in Romans 16:5b: The best manuscript tradition reads 'Asia' — the proconsular province in western Asia Minor comprising the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 and the sub-regions of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia, with Ephesus as the administrative capital. Epinetus was the first convert to Christ from this province, most likely led to faith by Paul during his Ephesian ministry.

9. Agapētos with the possessive genitive of egó indicates personal love, category three: Paul does not describe Epinetus merely as a fellow member of the royal family who receives impersonal love. He calls him 'my beloved friend' — the object of personal affection. This is one of the marks of Paul's intimate circle of spiritual companions, distinct from the general command to love all members of the royal family with impersonal love.

10. Epinetus represents the non-spectacular, consistently positive believer: His profile illustrates that spiritual growth is not the trajectory of a rocket but the slow, steady trot of a horse. He is the ordinary Christian who achieves the extraordinary through self-determined, daily positive volition toward doctrine. He did not require spectacular encouragement, visible recognition, or the continuous presence of his original teacher. He plugged. He persevered. He advanced to maturity. He had capacity for life — and capacity for dying.

Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Four

Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 16:6 “Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Pay my respects to Mary, who bestowed much labor on us.
Job 5:19–27 “He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you. You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season. Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: In six troubles he will deliver you; furthermore in seven, evil will not touch you. In famine he will preserve you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and you will not be afraid of destruction when it comes. At violent death and economic depression you will laugh, and from the wild beasts of the earth you have nothing to fear. For your covenant will be with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field will be at peace with you. You will know that your tent is in a state of prosperity, and you will visit your home and fear no loss. You will know also that your seed will be many, and your offspring like the young shoots of the field. You will come to the grave in full age, like a shock of corn comes in its season. Behold, this we have researched. Hear it and know it for yourself.

Romans 16 presents an honor roll of believers in Rome who attained maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Chapter 524 examines two subjects in sequence: first, the theological framework for dying grace drawn from Job 5:19–27, which the Royal Family Honor Code treats as the doctrinal foundation for understanding death as an extension of living; and second, the introduction of Mary of Rome in verse 6, whose designation as one who 'bestowed much labor on us' places her among the greatest women in the Pauline letters. The Job passage provides the doctrinal background; the Mary introduction illustrates its application in a life fully adjusted to the justice of God.

I. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Theology of Dying Grace

The Royal Family Honor Code, as developed in the preceding chapters of this commentary, contains a principle without parallel in any human system of ethics: dying is a component of living. The code asserts that if there is nothing worth living for, there is nothing worth dying for — and the converse holds with equal force. This principle does not diminish death; it integrates death into the total structure of the believer's life under the Protocol Plan of God.

In the ordinary viewpoint of the human race, living and dying are treated as separate and opposing realities. The honor code rejects this dichotomy. Living and dying are both components of a single life designed by the justice of God, and Bible doctrine resident in the soul is the instrument that prepares the believer for both. The same doctrine that sustains the believer through the pressures of daily life — economic reversal, military danger, social hostility — is the doctrine that transforms the dying phase into the greatest moment of blessing the believer will experience in time.

This framework rests on a precise understanding of what death is. At physical death, the soul and the human spirit depart from the body. The body remains; the immaterial components of the person — the soul bearing human life imputed at birth, and the human spirit bearing eternal life imputed at the new birth — pass into the presence of the Lord. The Apostle Paul states this precisely in 2 Corinthians 5: absent from the body, face to face with the Lord. This departure does not diminish perceptive ability; it intensifies it. The empirical sensory systems of the body — sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell — are removed, but the soul's rational and volitional capacities and the spirit's receptivity to God remain intact and are sharpened. Perception that was constrained by spatial and physical limitations is freed from those constraints.

One aspect of this transition is that at the moment of physical death, the soul and spirit briefly perceive the immediate physical environment before moving on — the battlefield, the accident scene, the room. This is not a theological novelty; it is a corollary of the doctrine that perceptive ability belongs to the immaterial person, not to the body. Leaving the body does not destroy that ability; it liberates and increases it.

The same principles apply, with inverted result, to the unbeliever. At physical death, the soul of the unbeliever — bearing human life but lacking eternal life — passes into torments, in preparation for the lake of fire. That soul retains complete perceptive ability. The intensification of experience that for the mature believer means intensified blessing means for the unbeliever an intensification of condemnation.

Every believer dies alone in the sense that is theologically decisive: neither loved ones nor enemies, neither friends nor antagonists, can add to or subtract from the inner resources with which the dying believer faces that transition. The body of mature believers surrounding a deathbed contributes nothing to the dying person's spiritual resources. Those resources were built, or not built, through years of consistent doctrine intake. This is why the honor code treats dying not as the negation of living but as its culminating expression.

II. Job 5:19–27 — Seven Categories of Dying Grace

Job 5:19–27 provides a systematic doctrinal framework for dying grace organized around seven categories of disaster and four concluding statements about the mature believer's death. The passage presupposes throughout what the commentary has designated the Z-radical category: the believer who has achieved maturity adjustment to the justice of God through sustained doctrine intake — supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace.

A. The Seven Troubles (Job 5:19)

The verse introduces the controlling number: six troubles and seven. In Hebrew numerical idiom, this sequence (n / n+1) does not enumerate specific disasters but describes completeness — every category of adversity that the mature believer may encounter. The assurance is categorical: in every form of trouble, deliverance is available; in every category of evil, evil will not ultimately dominate. The verb translated 'deliver' is the Cal perfect of natsal (נָצַל), which in the Hiphil stem denotes causative deliverance — God as primary cause, doctrine resident in the soul as secondary cause. The mechanism of deliverance is not raw divine omnipotence operating apart from the believer's spiritual state; it is the justice of God honoring the doctrine that the believer has accumulated through consistent gap function.

B. Economic Disaster — Famine (Job 5:20a)

'In famine he will preserve you from death.' The verb is the Cal perfect of padah (פָּדָה), meaning to redeem, to ransom, to lift out of a situation. The force is not merely preservation in the sense of survival at minimum level; it is extraction from the disaster itself. The ultimate tragedy of economic collapse — death by starvation, by want, by deprivation — does not overtake the mature believer. This is not a promise of material prosperity in every circumstance; it is a statement that the dying of the mature believer, whenever it comes and under whatever external conditions, will be characterized by blessing rather than by the catastrophe itself.

C. Military Danger — War (Job 5:20b)

'In war from the power of the sword.' The citizen soldier and the professional soldier alike face the adversary of the battlefield. Military competence, courage, and training are legitimate and valuable, but they cannot by themselves provide what the soul requires in extremis. Military integrity under pressure requires a foundation in divine integrity. That foundation is the link established through salvation adjustment, rebound, and consistent doctrine intake. The sword — the instrument of violent death in its ancient form, standing for every weapon system in every era — cannot terminate the mature believer's life outside of God's sovereign timing. Until that timing is reached, no weapon can touch the believer. When that timing arrives, death in combat is not a disaster but a transition into dying grace.

D. Social Hostility — The Scourge of the Tongue (Job 5:21)

'You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue.' The tongue as an instrument of social destruction is one of the most persistent categories of pressure in the believer's life. Slander, maligning, false reports, and misrepresentation produce social isolation, reputation damage, and relational rupture. The verb governing this clause is the Niphal imperfect of chaba (חָבָא), a passive stem: God himself, honoring the doctrine resident in the believer's soul, does the concealing. The believer is not hidden from the tongue's attack in the sense that attacks do not occur; the attacks occur. The believer is hidden from their ultimate power to destroy. The doctrine inside provides the stability that social hostility cannot penetrate.

E. Violent Death and Economic Depression — Laughing (Job 5:22)

'At violent death and economic depression you will laugh.' The verb is the Cal imperfect of sachaq (שָׂחַק), which does not describe the laughter of contempt or the forced laughter of bravado, but the relaxed laughter of genuine happiness — laughter at a celebration, laughter from inner contentment. This is the laughter of inner resources, not exterior resources. The believer facing violent death does not laugh because he has medical resources or because his circumstances are comfortable. He laughs because the doctrine resident in his soul produces a quality of inner happiness that the external situation cannot reach. The physical principle of relaxation reducing pain is an analogy: concentrated relaxation diminishes experienced pain; concentrated doctrine diminishes the experiential force of death and disaster.

F. Wild Animals as a Category of Violent Death (Job 5:22b–23)

The wild animals of the field represent a category of violent death common in the ancient world. The principle extends forward to every era's equivalent instruments of sudden death: accident, weaponry, natural disaster. The statement 'your covenant will be with the stones of the field' is a reference to ancient artillery — the sling and stone used in siege warfare and open combat. By metonymy, the passage encompasses every system of ballistic or explosive weaponry. 'The beasts of the field will be at peace with you' restates the principle: the timing of the mature believer's death is entirely in the hands of God, and until that timing arrives, no system of violence can remove the believer. When that timing arrives, the transition is one of grace.

G. God's Timing — Full Age (Job 5:26)

'You will come to the grave in full age, like a shock of corn comes in its season.' Full age (kelach, כֶּלַח) does not designate a chronological age. It designates the perfection of God's timing for each individual believer. Full age may be two hours after birth. It may be seven, twelve, twenty-one, forty, sixty, or one hundred years. The agricultural image of the corn shock gathered in its season emphasizes divine wisdom: the expert farmer knows the exact moment of harvest. God as the expert determines the exact moment of each believer's departure. The justice of God is the guarantee that this timing will always be perfect — that it will always be sufficient, that the doctrine available to the believer by that moment will always be adequate for dying grace.

III. The Four Concluding Blessings of Dying Grace (Job 5:24–27)

The passage concludes with four positive statements about what the mature believer knows and can anticipate. These are not promises extended to every believer but to the believer who has fulfilled the X-plus-Y-plus-Z framework — the complete structure of adjustment to the justice of God.

A. First Blessing — The Tent at Peace (Job 5:24a)

'You will know that your tent is in a state of prosperity.' The verb yada (יָדַע) in the Cal perfect denotes the cognitive certainty of the mature believer. The tent — the human body — is described as being in a state of prosperity and peace even at the point of death. This is the first hope of the X-plus-Y-plus-Z framework transposed into dying: the mature believer's body, however it dies, dies in the context of divine blessing.

B. Second Blessing — No Loss at Departure (Job 5:24b)

'You will visit your home and fear no loss.' The departure from this life is described as a visit to one's permanent home — heaven. The believer is not losing something irreplaceable by dying; the believer is arriving somewhere permanent. Fear of loss — loss of rewards, loss of eternal blessings — is excluded for the mature believer. Maximum adjustment to the justice of God means great reward and great decoration at the judgment seat of Christ. The mature believer goes home without the anxiety of empty hands.

C. Third Blessing — Blessing by Association for Those Left Behind (Job 5:25)

'You will know also that your seed will be many, and your offspring like the young shoots of the field.' The seed being many is an agricultural idiom for prosperity: the greater the sowing, the greater the harvest. Applied to the departing believer, it means that those left behind — spouse, children, parents, colleagues, those in every relational category — receive blessing by association with the mature believer who has died. This blessing extends to believers and unbelievers alike who were associated with the mature believer in life. The justice of God provides this blessing not because the survivors have earned it, but because they were in relationship with one who did.

D. Fourth Blessing — Perfect Timing Confirmed (Job 5:26)

The corn shock image seals the passage with the assurance that God's timing for each individual departure is perfect. The mature believer facing a prolonged dying process — weeks, months, a year — may encounter the temptation to bitterness as the process continues and others continue in health and activity. Those who love a dying believer may face the temptation to bitterness and self-pity on their own account. Doctrine is the only effective answer to both temptations. The capacity to grieve a loss honestly and fully, while refusing bitterness and self-pity, is one of the marks of the soul that has taken doctrine seriously over time. God always knows best. The timing of departure is in His wisdom, and that wisdom is always perfect.

E. The Conclusion of the Matter (Job 5:27)

'Behold, this we have researched. Hear it and know it for yourself.' The verb translated 'researched' is the Cal perfect of chaqar (חָקַר), meaning to investigate, to search out, to draw conclusions from gathered evidence. The process described is that of systematic doctrine intake accumulated over time: doctrine today, doctrine tomorrow, doctrine the next day, the facts drawn together and the conclusion reached. The conclusion is simple: dying is a part of living. Dying is the best part of living for the one who has doctrine. The critical phrase is 'know it for yourself' — the knowledge must be personally appropriated, not merely intellectually acknowledged. This is the distinction between gnosis and epignosis (ἐπίγνωσις): full, exact, internalized knowledge that has become operational in the soul.

IV. The Mechanics of Dying Grace — X Plus Y Plus Z

The doctrinal structure underlying dying grace is the full X-plus-Y-plus-Z framework of adjustment to the justice of God. Each stage of that framework produces a 'hope' — absolute confidence — in a category of divine blessing. The third hope, which pertains specifically to eternal rewards, is the framework within which dying grace operates.

X: Human life imputed at birth, plus Adam's original sin imputed at birth — establishing condemnation as the precondition for salvation. Plus pertinent doctrine: Christ bearing our sins on the cross, reconciliation, propitiation, redemption. This yields the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. Plus the reality of salvation adjustment — believing in Christ, the moment of judicial imputation of divine righteousness and the forgiveness of all sins.

Y: The second potential — receiving great blessing in time at and after the point of maturity. Plus pertinent doctrine accumulated through consistent gap function. This yields the second hope: absolute confidence that consistent doctrine intake will crack the maturity barrier. Plus maturity adjustment to the justice of God — the Z-radical position.

Z: The third potential — great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. Plus pertinent doctrine, plus undeserved suffering responded to with doctrine. This yields the third hope: absolute confidence of great decoration and blessing in eternity. This is the 'good' of 1 Timothy 2:10 — the attainment of maturity status through the consistent function of doctrine, love, experiential sanctification, and stability of mind.

The believer who has not built this structure — who has been casual or negative toward doctrine — is not prepared for dying. The dying phase will be characterized by the absence of inner resources at the moment they are most needed. The believer who has built this structure finds that dying is the moment when every line of doctrine absorbed over a lifetime comes into its fullest operational expression. The inner resources do not fail at the point of greatest pressure; they are activated by it.

V. The Rapture Exception and the Universal Applicability of the Framework

One category of believer will not pass through physical death: the rapture generation. As 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 states, the Lord himself will descend with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, the dead in Christ will rise first, and then those who are alive at that moment will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air. For the rapture generation, the transition from mortal existence to resurrection body bypasses the physical dying process entirely.

This exception does not void the framework; it confirms it. The rapture generation requires the same doctrine, the same adjustment to the justice of God, the same Z-radical maturity as every other generation. The absence of a physical dying phase does not remove the need for inner resources — it simply removes one specific context in which those resources are tested. The framework of X-plus-Y-plus-Z applies to every Church Age believer without exception.

VI. Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome

With the doctrinal framework of dying grace established from Job 5, the commentary returns to Romans 16:6 and the introduction of Mary of Rome.

A. The Greeting Formula

Paul opens with the aorist active imperative of aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι): pay my respects to, salute, greet. The aorist tense contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety — a decisive, complete act of respect. The active voice indicates Paul as the one producing the action. The imperative mood here is the imperative of entreaty rather than command: the force is a request, not an order. The object is the accusative singular from the proper noun Maria (Μαρία), the Greek form of the name rendered in English as Mary.

B. Which Mary?

The New Testament contains at least six women named Mary: Mary the mother of the humanity of Christ; Mary Magdalene; Mary the sister of Lazarus and Martha; Mary the wife of Clopas; Mary the mother of John Mark; and the Mary of Romans 16:6. This final Mary is identified nowhere else in the New Testament. She is mentioned in this verse alone. She is not connected by the text to any of the other five. Everything that can be known about her is contained in the phrase that follows her name.

The absence of further identification is itself significant. Paul does not need to identify her by relationship or location to convey his estimate of her. Her presence on this honor roll communicates the essential fact: she has attained maturity adjustment to the justice of God. She is listed in the company of Phoebe, Prisca, and the other women of Romans 16 who cracked the maturity barrier. The number of women on this honor roll is remarkable and carries a clear doctrinal implication: nothing prevents a woman from attaining maximum spiritual maturity except her own negative volition toward doctrine.

C. 'Who Bestowed Much Labor on Us'

The description of Mary is precise and theologically dense. The verb is the aorist active indicative of kopiao (κοπιάω), meaning to labor to the point of exhaustion, to work with intense and sustained effort. This is not ordinary activity; it is the vocabulary of maximum exertion. The cognate noun kopos (κόπος) is used elsewhere in the Pauline letters to describe apostolic labor and the work of doctrine communication. When Paul applies this term to Mary, he is assigning to her activity the highest category of spiritual labor.

The prepositional phrase 'on us' — or in some manuscript traditions 'on you' — indicates that Mary's labor was directed toward the benefit of others: the congregation, the believing community, those associated with her. This is the outward expression of Z-radical maturity. The believer who has accumulated maximum doctrine and achieved maximum adjustment to the justice of God does not retain the blessing privately; it overflows into labor for others, producing blessing by association in those around her.

D. Inner Beauty and the Mature Woman — 1 Timothy 2:9–15

Mary of Rome stands as an example of the inner beauty described in 1 Timothy 2:9–15. That passage commands women to make themselves beautiful — not primarily through external adornment, though respectable and well-arranged clothing is appropriate — but through right thinking, soundness of mind, and doctrine resident in the soul. The argument of the passage is that beauty is not a matter of physical symmetry or external decoration but of the inner life of the soul. The soul, not the body, is the source of genuine beauty.

The conclusion of the passage at 1 Timothy 2:15 states that women who persist in doctrine, impersonal love, experiential sanctification, and stability of mind attain the maturity status described as 'the good' — the Z-radical condition. This is the condition Mary of Rome has attained.

The phrase translated 'stability of mind' is sophrosyne (σωφροσύνη), meaning soundness of mind, self-mastery through right thinking, the capacity to think clearly and act consistently because the thinking of doctrine governs the soul. This is the inner dynamic that produces genuine beauty in the woman. It is also the inner dynamic that produces dying grace: the believer whose soul is governed by doctrine faces death with the same stability she brought to every other pressure of life.

The full exposition of Mary's labor and its significance will be developed in the following chapter. What the present chapter establishes is the doctrinal framework within which any such labor must be understood: a woman who has fulfilled X-plus-Y-plus-Z, whose soul contains the doctrine necessary for living with maximum blessing and dying with even greater blessing, whose labor for others is the natural overflow of that adjustment, and who stands on this honor roll because Paul — the greatest believer who ever lived — considered her worthy of his personal respect.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Four

1. Dying is a component of living, not its negation. The Royal Family Honor Code treats physical death as an extension of the believer's life under the Protocol Plan of God. The same doctrine that sustains the believer through economic, military, and social pressures is the doctrine that transforms the dying phase into the believer's greatest moment of blessing.

2. Bible doctrine is the mechanism of dying grace. The justice of God honors doctrine resident in the soul and delivers the mature believer through every category of disaster enumerated in Job 5:19–27. God is the primary cause of deliverance; doctrine in the soul is the secondary cause. The mechanism is not raw divine power exercised apart from the believer's spiritual state.

3. At physical death, perceptive ability is increased, not destroyed. The soul and the human spirit depart from the body at physical death, leaving the body behind. The empirical sensory systems of the body cease; but the immaterial person's perceptive capacity is sharpened. The believer becomes absent from the body and face to face with the Lord, knowing God even as the believer is currently known by Him.

4. Every believer dies alone in the theologically decisive sense. No other person — whether friend, loved one, or community — can contribute to or subtract from the inner resources the dying believer possesses. Those resources were built through years of consistent doctrine intake. This is why the honor code insists that doctrine must be the priority of every day, not a resource reserved for crisis.

5. God's timing for the death of the mature believer is always perfect. Full age in Job 5:26 does not designate a chronological age; it designates the perfection of divine wisdom applied to each individual believer's departure. The justice of God guarantees that by the moment of death, every mature believer will have accumulated sufficient doctrine for dying grace — whether that moment comes in infancy, youth, middle age, or old age.

6. Dying grace produces blessing by association for those left behind. Job 5:25 states that the seed of the mature believer will be many. This is an agricultural idiom for prosperity flowing outward from the departed believer to those who were in relationship with that believer in life. The justice of God provides this blessing by association to survivors — believers and unbelievers alike — as the heritage of the mature believer's life.

7. Mary of Rome attained maximum adjustment to the justice of God. Romans 16:6 identifies her by a single description: she bestowed much labor on us. The verb kopiao designates intense, exhausting spiritual labor — the vocabulary Paul applies to apostolic and doctrinal work. That Paul lists her on this honor roll and assigns this description to her places her among the greatest women in the Pauline letters. Her labor is the outward expression of Z-radical maturity.

8. Nothing prevents a woman from attaining maximum spiritual maturity except negative volition. The number of women on the Romans 16 honor roll demonstrates that the Z-radical position is equally available to women. The inner beauty described in 1 Timothy 2:9–15 — right thinking, soundness of mind, doctrine resident in the soul — is the same dynamic that produces dying grace. The mature woman, like the mature man, faces death with inner resources that the external situation cannot reach.

9. Epignosis, not gnosis, is the knowledge required for dying grace. The Job 5:27 imperative — 'hear it and know it for yourself' — points to the distinction between intellectual acknowledgment and internalized operational knowledge. Epignosis is the full, exact, personally appropriated knowledge that becomes functional in the soul under pressure. Casual or occasional doctrine intake produces gnosis at best; consistent daily intake through gap function produces the epignosis that functions in the dying phase.

10. The X-plus-Y-plus-Z framework culminates in the third hope — dying grace. The first hope is absolute confidence of eternal life through faith in Christ. The second hope is absolute confidence of great blessing in time through maturity adjustment. The third hope is absolute confidence of great reward and decoration at the judgment seat of Christ. It is the third hope that is operative at the moment of physical death. The believer who has fulfilled the full framework goes home without anxiety and leaves behind, for those still living, the blessing by association that is the heritage of every life fully adjusted to the justice of God.

In the Hiphil stem, a causative: God as primary cause delivers, with doctrine resident in the soul as secondary cause. The deliverance is categorical — in every category of trouble, in every form of disaster, the mature believer is delivered.

Applied to economic disaster (famine): the mature believer is not merely preserved at minimum level but lifted out of the catastrophe. The dying of the mature believer, under whatever external conditions, is characterized by blessing rather than by the disaster itself.
sachaq שָׂחַק sachaq — to laugh in relaxation, to laugh at a celebration Cal imperfect in Job 5:22. Distinguished from laughter of contempt or bravado. Denotes the relaxed laughter of genuine inner happiness — the response to violent death and economic depression by one whose inner resources of doctrine are greater than any external pressure.
sophrosyne σωφροσύνη sophrosyne — soundness of mind, stability of thought, self-mastery through right thinking Used in 1 Timothy 2:9, 15 in connection with the beauty of the mature woman. Denotes the capacity to think clearly and act consistently because the thinking of doctrine governs the soul. The inner dynamic that produces genuine beauty in the woman and, by the same mechanism, produces the stability required for dying grace.
