In this state the believer cannot apply doctrine, cannot exercise genuine love, and is susceptible to manipulation by smooth words and flattery. The Proverbs 18:8 image of gossip descending into the chambers of the belly illustrates its self-destructive dynamic: prolonged emotional revolt produces progressive corrosion of the soul analogous to a peptic ulcer.

Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Four

Romans 16:18 — The Doctrine of Emotion: Anatomy, Dispensations, and Emotional Revolt of the Soul

Romans 16:17–18 “I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Now I urge you, brethren, look out for those who are causing dissensions and apostasies contrary to the doctrine which you have learned from a teacher. In fact, be turning away from them — be separating from them. For such believers do not obey or serve our Lord Christ, but their own emotions serving themselves. And by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the right lobes of the unsuspecting, that is, believers who are ignorant of doctrine.

Romans 16:18 continues the command to identify and separate from reversionistic believers whose influence promotes dissension and apostasy. Paul's indictment turns on a single diagnosis: such persons serve not Christ but their own emotions. This chapter develops the Doctrine of Emotion in full, treating its anatomical background in Scripture, its relationship to the dispensations of the Church Age and the Millennium, its potential for revolt against the soul's proper order, and its exploitation by false teachers through smooth and flattering speech.

I. Three Anatomical Words for Emotion in Scripture

Scripture uses words drawn from human anatomy to describe invisible realities of the soul. Just as the physical heart serves as the biblical term for the right lobe — the thinking center of the soul — three anatomical terms designate the seat of emotion: bowels (intestines), belly, and reins (kidneys). All three share a common structural feature: they are hollow, sack-like organs. This physical characteristic mirrors the nature of emotion itself — an empty responder that contains no thought, no rationality, no doctrine, and no capacity to generate wisdom.

A. Bowels and Belly

The bowels and belly appear in contexts where Scripture describes the seat of intense feeling. Their function as hollow, waste-bearing organs underscores the theological point: when the emotions are filled with something other than doctrine-driven responses, they are filled with what is worthless. In 2 Corinthians 6:11–12, the Apostle Paul addresses the Corinthians directly:

2 Corinthians 6:11–12 “We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: O Corinthians — our mouth has been opened face to face with you, and our right lobes have been enlarged. You have not been hindered from growth by us, but you are being hindered by your own emotions.

Paul and his associates — Apollos, Timothy, Titus — provided four of the finest Bible teachers available in the first century. Yet the Corinthians remained spiritually stunted. The hindrance was not deficient teaching but their own emotion-dominated souls. The intestines, as the anatomical image, communicate that the emotions had become a receptacle for waste rather than a responder to doctrine. The gift of communication, however brilliantly expressed, is rendered inert when the receptor is choked with emotional content rather than doctrinal content.

B. The Reins — Kidneys and Adrenal Glands

The third anatomical term is the reins, from the Hebrew kilya (כִּלְיָה), meaning the fat pads that cover and protect the kidneys. The term refers by extension to the kidneys themselves and to the adrenal glands that rest upon them. The adrenal glands secrete epinephrine — the hormone of fright, flight, and fight — which increases pulse rate, cardiac output, blood flow to the muscles, and blood glucose. When Scripture speaks of the reins as the seat of emotion, it is pointing precisely at this physiological apparatus: the adrenaline-producing glands that drive the body's most intense emotional responses.

Several Psalms and prophetic texts pair the reins with the heart (right lobe) as the two poles of the soul's inner life:

Psalm 7:9 “Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous — you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Let the evil of the reversionist come to an end, but establish the righteousness of the mature believer. For the righteous God tests the right lobe and the emotions.
Psalm 26:2 “Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Examine me, O Lord, and test me — test my emotions and my right lobe.
Jeremiah 11:20 “But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind...” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But O Lord of the armies who judges righteously with integrity, who tests the emotions and the right lobe.
Jeremiah 17:10 “I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: I the Lord search the right lobe. I test the emotions, even to give to every man according to his modus vivendi.

The consistent pairing of right lobe and reins across these texts establishes a theological anthropology: the soul has a male part (the right lobe, the thinking center) and a female part (the emotion, the responder). The right lobe contains the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary, categorical storage, and norms and standards of the conscience. The emotion contains none of these. It responds to what the right lobe provides — to doctrine, to music, to beauty, to patriotism, to the many legitimate stimuli of human experience. When the emotion responds to a right-lobe governed by doctrine, the soul is normal and functional. When the emotion revolts and takes command, the soul is disordered.

A pathological analogy clarifies the disorder. A pheochromocytoma is a tumor of the adrenal glands that causes the uncontrolled secretion of epinephrine without regulation by the central nervous system. The result is severe hypertension, anxiety, nausea, and cardiac stress — physiological instability driven by uncontrolled adrenaline. This medical condition is a precise physical analogue of emotional revolt of the soul: emotion producing its responses without any governing check from doctrine resident in the right lobe.

II. Emotion and Spirituality Across the Dispensations

A critical error in popular Christianity is the identification of spiritual experience with emotional or ecstatic experience. This error is corrected by relating emotion to the specific dispensation under consideration. Two dispensations are relevant: the Church Age and the Millennium.

A. The Church Age

The Church Age is the dispensation of the royal family of God. At the moment of salvation, every believer is permanently indwelt by the Holy Spirit. Thereafter, the believer has the option of the filling of the Spirit through the rebound technique — naming known sins to God (1 John 1:9) — which restores fellowship instantly. The following principles govern emotion and spirituality in this dispensation:

1. Spirituality in the Church Age is the filling of the Holy Spirit, and it carries no emotional connotation. Spirituality is Spirit-filling minus ecstatics. The filling of the Spirit produces the character and knowledge of Christ through the perception of doctrine, not through emotional experience.

2. The Holy Spirit did not indwell all believers in any previous dispensation. The universal indwelling and the availability of the filling of the Spirit are unique to the Church Age. This makes the present dispensation the greatest of all dispensations — one of aristocracy, in which every born-again believer is a permanent member of the royal family of God.

3. Appreciation of the Lord Jesus Christ comes through the perception of doctrine rather than through emotional function. Emotion is not eliminated — it is restored to its proper role as a responder to doctrine in the right lobe.

4. Emotional function cannot produce integrity. It cannot fulfill the honor code of the Christian way of life. It cannot think or apply doctrine. It simply responds. There is often stimulation and sometimes reaction in the function of emotion, but emotion is not a constituent of the filling of the Holy Spirit.

5. In this dispensation, emotion is a responder to many things in the right lobe, including doctrine, patriotism, the laws of establishment, and love in all its categories. But emotional response is never equivalent to the filling of the Holy Spirit, and is never the index of one's spiritual status.

6. Depression does not indicate loss of the filling of the Spirit. Many forms of depression are physiologically induced — by medical conditions, by medication, by neurological imbalance. A believer may be physiologically depressed and simultaneously advancing spiritually and filled with the Spirit. How one feels has nothing whatever to do with one's spiritual status quo.

7. Emotion and ecstatics have no spiritual content in the Church Age. Emotion is an empty responder. Therefore, how one feels is never the index of spiritual life or spiritual experience.

8. Emotional activity or ecstatics is not indicative of spiritual activity or advance in the Christian life. Movements that make ecstatic experience the criterion of spirituality misunderstand both the nature of emotion and the nature of the Spirit's filling.

9. The purpose of the filling of the Spirit is the perception of doctrine, advance to maturity, and production from the royal ambassadorship — never the manufacture of an emotional or ecstatic state. No ecstatics; no emotion as criterion.

10. Emotion is designed to respond to doctrine in the right lobe, but emotion is not characteristic of the filling of the Spirit. Ecstatic responses — to music, to athletic achievement, to personal victories — belong to the human race in general. The filling of the Spirit belongs specifically to the believer in fellowship. The two can coexist without being identical.

B. The Millennium

The Millennium is the thousand-year reign of Christ on earth following the Second Advent. Human history began in perfect environment — the Garden of Eden — and terminates in perfect environment — the Millennial Kingdom. The Millennium demonstrates conclusively that environment, even perfect environment, solves nothing. Despite universal prosperity, peace, and the personal reign of the Lord Jesus Christ, revolution erupts at the end of the thousand years. The solution to man's problems is never environmental; it is relational — relationship with God through faith in Christ, relationship fulfilled in the plan of God, relationship consummated in resurrection. The following principles govern emotion and spirituality in the Millennium:

1. Only in the Millennium, when Christ is personally present on earth, does ecstatics legitimately characterize the filling of the Spirit. Where the Church Age is spirituality minus ecstatics, the Millennium is spirituality plus ecstatics.

2. The Millennium is the only other dispensation besides the Church Age in which all believers are universally indwelt by the Spirit and commanded to be controlled by the Spirit (Ezekiel 36:27; 37:14; Jeremiah 31:33).

3. In the Millennium, the filling of the Spirit is used to appreciate the reigning Christ in His visible presence. Emotional and ecstatic response to the Lord's personal reign is therefore a legitimate expression of Spirit-filling.

4. Believers in the Millennium are also commanded to be filled with the Spirit (Isaiah 29:19; 32:15; 44:3; Ezekiel 39:29; Zechariah 12:10).

5. The filling of the Spirit in the Millennium is characterized by ecstatics and emotional appreciation, as prophesied in Joel 2:28–29. This ecstatic dimension is dispensationally specific to the Millennium and cannot be transferred as a norm to the Church Age.

III. Emotional Revolt of the Soul

Emotional revolt of the soul is one of the identifiable stages of reversionism — the retrograde spiritual regression by which a believer abandons positive volition toward doctrine and moves back toward the patterns and values of the old sin nature.

1. Instead of responding to doctrine resident in the soul, the emotion revolts and takes command. Negative volition toward doctrine eventuates in the emotion — the empty, hollow responder — seizing control of the soul. Since the emotion contains no doctrine, no rationality, and no common sense, the soul is now governed by a faculty incapable of thought.

2. With emotion in command of the soul, all capacity for life is forfeited. There is no capacity for love, no capacity for happiness, and no capacity for divine blessing in the state of emotional revolt of the soul.

3. Negative volition toward doctrine, combined with the consequent recession of doctrinal content, is replaced by the frantic search for happiness and total dependence on feeling rather than rational thought. This dynamic explains the attraction of chemical substitutes: when thought has been rejected and the emotion finds nothing in the right lobe to respond to, a chemical stimulus is sought to produce the sensation of feeling. Drugs are instruments of therapy and medicine, not vehicles for the search for happiness.

4. Having lost the capacity to respond normally to the right lobe, the emotion in revolt becomes inflexible regarding non-essentials. Revelation 2:23 states: 'I am the one investigating the emotions and the right lobe, and I will give to each according to your actions in this area.' The Lord's evaluation of the soul addresses precisely the question of which faculty governs — the right lobe with its doctrine, or the emotion in revolt.

5. Emotion as a responder contributes to capacity for life; emotion as a leader destroys it. As a responder and follower, emotion intensifies capacity for love, for happiness, and for meaningful human experience (Genesis 43:30; 1 Kings 3:26; Philippians 1:8; 1 John 3:17; Proverbs 23:16). As a reactor that generates its own agenda, it produces loss of capacity, loss of motivation, and loss of spiritual momentum (Jeremiah 4:19; Lamentations 1:20; 2:11).

Jeremiah's experience illustrates the mature believer's proper orientation when emotion is under pressure. When a plot was organized against his life, Jeremiah did not capitulate to panic or to the frantic reaction of an emotion-governed soul. He appealed instead to the Supreme Court of Heaven:

Jeremiah 11:19–20 “But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes... But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: And I, like a pet household lamb, have been led to the slaughter — but I did not know that they had organized a plot against me: 'We will destroy the tree with his food; we will cut him off from the land of the living, that his name will never again be remembered.' But O Lord of the armies who judges with integrity, who tests the emotions and the right lobe — let me see justice on them, for to you I have committed my cause.

Jeremiah was a mature believer who had advanced to the point where he could appeal to the Supreme Court of Heaven and receive justice. His emotion did not govern his response; his doctrine-laden right lobe did. Those who sought to assassinate him were killed; he lived for many years thereafter.

IV. Exegesis of Romans 16:18b — Smooth and Flattering Speech

The second half of verse 18 describes the instrument by which emotionally reversionistic teachers extend their influence: linguistic manipulation disguised as spiritual sincerity.

A. Chrēstologia — Smooth Speech

The first term is the compound noun chrēstologia (χρηστολογία), from the prepositional phrase dia plus the ablative of chrēstologia. The adjective chrēstos (χρηστός) means good or pleasant — not the proper name Christ. Combined with logos (λόγος) for speech, the compound means pleasant speech, bland speech, smooth and gentle non-irritating speech that masks a fraudulent purpose. The ablative of means with dia signals that this smooth speech is the instrument by which the deception is accomplished — means accompanied by source. Corrected translation: by their smooth speech, smooth speech in the sense of hypocrisy.

B. Eulogia — Flattering Speech

The second term, joined by the connective kai (καί), extending the prepositional phrase, is the ablative of means of eulogia (εὐλογία). The adverb eu (εὖ) means well or good; logia means communication. Together: good communication, or in this context, flattering speech. Only doctrine resident in the soul provides a defense against flattery. Flattery appeals to arrogance, and arrogance lies just beneath the veneer of false humility. The reversionistic false teacher approaches with apparent spiritual enthusiasm, employing smooth and flattering speech to recruit the doctrinally uninformed.

C. Exapataō — They Deceive

The verb is the present active indicative of exapataō (ἐξαπατάω), a compound of ex (from) and apataō (to seduce or deceive). To deceive from — to seduce away from truth into error. The present tense is a customary present, describing what habitually occurs when a believer is either uninstructed in doctrine or negative toward it. The active voice: reversionistic false teachers and apostate witnesses produce the action. The indicative mood is the potential indicative — what happens to the believer who is negative toward doctrinal teaching. He becomes the vulnerable target for this form of manipulation.

D. Kardias tōn Akakōn — The Right Lobes of the Unsuspecting

The direct object is the accusative plural of kardia (καρδία), heart — the right lobe where thought exists. Just as the physiological heart circulates blood, the soul's heart circulates thought. The possessive genitive plural of akakos (ἄκακος) describes the victims. The adjective means innocent or unsuspecting — used of newborn children who are ignorant, lacking discernment. Here it describes believers who are ignorant of doctrine. Doctrine resident in the soul produces discernment; absence of doctrine produces vulnerability. Those who are ignorant of doctrine are taken in by flattery, by false humility, and by all the pseudo-spiritual veneers of religious emotionalism.

V. Principles from Romans 16:17–18

1. The weak believer or reversionist who is the subject of these verses is not authority-oriented. To the degree that arrogance governs the soul, authority is rejected. Military basic training illustrates the corrective principle: a rigorous training system that removes arrogance produces authority orientation in believer and non-believer alike.

2. The weak believer or reversionist of this passage seeks to build a mutual admiration society — a network of emotional validation that substitutes for doctrinal community.

3. Spiritual authority begins with God and continues through delegated authority: the Word of God plus the pastor-teacher who communicates it.

4. The weak reversionist rejects the authority of both the Word and the pastor who communicates it. This dual rejection cuts the believer off from the only channels through which doctrine can enter the soul.

5. Because of this rejection, the weak reversionist does not serve or obey the Lord Christ. He is negative toward doctrine. He therefore has neither the motivation nor the momentum to advance in the plan of God.

6. It is therefore inevitable that the weak reversionist will, in his arrogance, be a slave to his emotion and thereby serve himself rather than the Lord. Even the finest Bible teaching — as demonstrated by the Apostle Paul, Apollos, Timothy, and Titus with the Corinthians — produces no effect where emotion is the criterion and arrogance is the motivator (2 Corinthians 6:11–12).

7. All emotional-type reversionists are motivated by arrogance. They have no authority orientation. To be motivated by arrogance is to be spiritually blind, non-perceptive in the soul.

8. Rejection of doctrine produces arrogance in the soul, and arrogance makes one susceptible to flattery and false teaching. The arrogant, non-authority-oriented believer is the unsuspecting target: he may not be consciously aware of his own arrogance, but it is present and operative, leaving him without resistance to smooth and flattering speech.

9. Believers ignorant of doctrine are impressed by pleasant personality and by emphasizing personality in their assessment of teachers. They become easily susceptible to flattery, having removed every vestige of doctrinal resistance.

10. When a vacuum is created in the soul through lack of doctrine, it is filled by emotion as the criterion and arrogance as the motivator. This explains the persistent popularity of religious movements that prioritize ecstatic experience over doctrinal content. Fundamentalist Christianity has too often traded its doctrinal heritage for an emotional substitute, producing souls wide open to exactly the deception Paul warns against in Romans 16:18.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Four

1. Emotion is the responder-faculty of the soul, anatomically depicted in Scripture by the bowels, belly, and reins (kidneys and adrenal glands). It is a hollow, sack-like faculty that contains no doctrine, no rationality, and no capacity to generate thought or wisdom.

2. The right lobe (heart) is the soul's thinking center; the emotion is the soul's responding center. A normal soul is one in which the right lobe, governed by doctrine, directs the responses of the emotion. An abnormal soul is one in which the emotion has revolted and taken command.

3. In the Church Age, spirituality — the filling of the Holy Spirit — carries no emotional or ecstatic connotation. Spiritual advance occurs through the perception of doctrine, not through the intensity of emotional experience. How one feels has nothing whatever to do with one's spiritual status quo.

4. In the Millennium, because Christ is personally present on earth, ecstatic emotional response legitimately characterizes the filling of the Spirit. This is dispensationally specific and cannot be imported into Church Age spirituality.

5. Emotional revolt of the soul is a stage of reversionism in which negative volition toward doctrine allows the emotion to seize control of the soul. All capacity for life, love, happiness, and blessing is forfeited in this condition.

6. The frantic search for happiness through chemical or ecstatic stimulation is a predictable consequence of emotional revolt. When the right lobe has been emptied of doctrine, the emotion seeks external stimulation to compensate for the absence of legitimate doctrinal response.

7. Reversionistic false teachers exploit the emotion-governed soul through two instruments: smooth speech (chrēstologia — bland, hypocrisy-masked pleasantness) and flattering speech (eulogia — communication crafted to appeal to the listener's arrogance). Doctrine resident in the soul is the only effective defense against these tactics.

8. The victims are described as akakos — the unsuspecting, those who are innocent of doctrinal content and therefore without discernment. Ignorance of doctrine does not produce humility; it produces arrogance and susceptibility to flattery.

9. Arrogance and emotion are mutually reinforcing. Arrogance rejects authority; without authority-orientation, doctrine cannot enter the soul; without doctrine, the emotion has nothing to respond to; the emotion therefore revolts and governs; arrogance is intensified. The cycle is broken only by positive volition toward doctrinal teaching.

10. The corrected translation of Romans 16:17–18 reads: 'Now I urge you, brethren, look out for those who are causing dissensions and apostasies contrary to the doctrine which you have learned from a teacher. In fact, be turning away from them — be separating from them. For such believers do not obey or serve our Lord Christ, but their own emotions serving themselves. And by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the right lobes of the unsuspecting, that is, believers who are ignorant of doctrine.'

Reversionism Retroactive spiritual regression — the condition of a believer who, through sustained negative volition toward doctrine, returns to the thinking, values, and behavior patterns of the old sin nature. Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Five

Romans 16:19 — Authority Orientation; the Gift of Tongues; Separation from Reversionists

Romans 16:17–19 “I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Now I urge you, brethren, look out for those who are causing dissensions and apostasies contrary to doctrine — doctrine which you have learned from a teacher. In fact, be turning away, be separating from them. For such believers do not serve or obey our Lord Christ, but their own emotions, serving themselves, and by means of their smooth and flattering speech they, the reversionists, deceive the right lobes of the unsuspecting. Certainly the report of your obedience has become known to all.

Romans 16 has brought us to the apostle Paul's concluding instructions to the Roman churches — three congregations, all meeting in private homes, all characterized by authority orientation. In verses 17–18, covered in the preceding chapter, Paul commanded separation from reversionists who cause dissensions and apostasies. Verse 19 opens with Paul's confident affirmation that the Roman believers are already authority-oriented, which is the very capacity that makes the drill of separation possible. The present chapter examines the grammatical structure of verse 19, the doctrine of authority orientation, and the extended doctrinal context: the gift of tongues as a historical warning sign to Israel, its cessation in AD 70, and its post-canonical perpetuation as a satanic counterfeit.

I. Exegesis of Romans 16:19a — The Report of Obedience

The Inferential Conjunction

The clause opens with the post-positive inferential conjunction gar (γάρ). Here it introduces a self-evident conclusion and functions as a strong affirmation of Paul's confidence. The particle is rendered certainly rather than the colourless for, so as to capture the force of the apostle's settled conviction.

The Subject — hupakoe

The nominative singular noun hupakoe (ὑπακοή) means a report or obedience. Its genitive pronoun, second person plural, specifies the Roman believers as the subjects: your obedience. The noun is built on akoē (ἀκοή, hearing, report) prefixed by hupo (ὑπό, under). Obedience is literally responsiveness under legitimate authority — the structural foundation of the royal family honor code.

The Verb — aphikneomai

The verb is aorist middle indicative of the compound aphikneomai (ἀφικνέομαι), formed from apo (ἀπό) + hikneōmai (ἱκνέομαι, to come, to arrive). It means to reach or to become known to. The aorist is a dramatic aorist: it states a present reality with the certitude of a completed past event, used here for emphasis as Paul, in greeting these mature believers, suddenly recognizes what they share in common. The middle voice is an indirect middle, highlighting the believers themselves — as agents of authority orientation — as producing the action. The indicative mood is declarative, affirming historical reality.

The Prepositional Phrase

The accusative plural eis pantas (εἰς πάντας) — preposition eis (εἰς) plus adjective pas (πᾶς) — means to all or to everyone. The corrected translation of the full clause: Certainly, the report of your obedience has become known to all.

II. The Doctrine of Authority Orientation

The apostle's confidence that the Roman believers could execute the command of separation rested entirely on their authority orientation. Authority orientation is the recognition that legitimate authority and genuine freedom are not in conflict: they mesh together to produce capacity for life and blessing. Everything of lasting worth in the believer's life is related to the proper functioning of authority. Reversionism, by contrast, is characterized by hostility to authority — the product of arrogance, emotional domination of the soul, and the vacuum that draws in false doctrine.

The normal soul is structured so that the right lobe — the area of doctrine, rational judgment, and values — governs the emotions. When emotion dominates the soul instead, the believer becomes susceptible to every form of reversionism. The reversionists described in verses 17–18 gain their influence not through sound argument but through smooth and flattering speech directed at believers whose doctrine is thin and whose emotions are therefore ungoverned. The antidote is authority orientation built through consistent, sustained intake of Bible doctrine.

The three Roman congregations — Priscilla and Aquila's house church, the assembly at the house of Aristobulus, and the group at the house of Narcissus — share this quality. Paul's confidence in them is not flattery: it is the apostolic recognition of a spiritually mature pattern that has become widely known. It is precisely this pattern that makes the command of verse 17 —

be turning away, be separating from them — executable without bitterness, vindictiveness, or implacability. Impersonal love can separate cleanly because it does not require the other person to change in order for the believer to be at peace. Separation under the honor code is a drill, not an explosion.

III. The Historical Function of the Gift of Tongues

Israel as Client Nation and the Transition of Dispensations

The command to separate from those who practise contemporary tongues requires understanding what the gift of tongues actually was, when it was legitimate, and when it ceased. From the time of Moses to AD 30, the Jewish nation functioned as the client nation to God. The Jews were the custodians of the written Word of God; with two possible exceptions, every human writer of both Testaments was Jewish. Their national responsibility included evangelism of the Gentiles and the maintenance of a missionary enterprise to preserve the knowledge of the God of Israel throughout history.

There had to come a time when that arrangement would change. The transition was not instantaneous or unannounced. God provided a forty-year warning period — from the Day of Pentecost in June AD 30 to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in August AD 70 — during which Israel would be evangelized in Gentile languages as a sign that the fifth cycle of discipline was approaching and that the age of Israel was being suspended. The gift of tongues was the instrument of that warning.

Old Testament Prophecy — Isaiah 28:11

The gift of tongues was prophesied in Isaiah 28:11. The historical context was the northern kingdom during a period of severe apostasy; drunkenness was epidemic and the speech of the intoxicated had become a cultural marker. Isaiah employed that image to deliver a devastating oracle: as you cannot understand the slurred speech of your own drunks, so God will speak to this people in a foreign language they have refused to receive. The text reads: with alien articulation and by means of a foreign language he will communicate doctrine to this people. This prophecy was quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 14:21–22, where he establishes its application to the church age: the gift of tongues was a sign not to those who believe but to unbelievers — specifically, to unbelieving Israel.

The Seven Feasts and the Church Age Interval

The Jewish festival calendar embedded the structure of redemptive history. The Passover portrayed the death of Christ in April AD 30. The Feast of Unleavened Bread, following immediately, portrayed fellowship with the Lord through doctrine. The Feast of First Fruits — the first Sunday after Passover — portrayed the resurrection of Christ, the basis of the believer's resurrection body and eternal fellowship. Pentecost, fifty days after First Fruits, marked the beginning of the church age.

After Pentecost there was a gap of over three months before the next cluster of feasts — Trumpets (the regathering of Israel at the second advent), Atonement (the restoration of regenerate Israel in fulfillment of the unconditional covenants), and Tabernacles (the millennium). That gap in the festival calendar was designed by God to represent the insertion of the church age. During the church age the age of Israel is suspended; the royal family of God is called out from both Jews and Gentiles; and no Jewish nation can function as a client nation to God. The times of the Gentiles have replaced the times of Israel until the second advent restores Israel to her covenant position.

The gift of tongues was the living signal of this transition. It operated from June AD 30 to August AD 70 — forty years — and it gave every generation of Jews in that period the opportunity to recognize that the dispensation had changed and that Jesus Christ, the God of Israel, was their only hope.

The Day of Pentecost — Acts 2:1–11

Acts 2 records the inauguration of the gift. When the sound came from heaven like a violent rushing wind and tongues as of fire appeared and distributed themselves on the assembled believers, they began to speak in foreign languages as the Spirit gave them the ability. The recipients in the crowd were Jewish pilgrims gathered from every Gentile nation under heaven — people whose native languages were no longer Hebrew or Aramaic but Parthian, Median, Elamite, Mesopotamian, Cappadocian, Pontian, Asian Greek, Phrygian, Pamphylian, Egyptian, Cyrenian, Latin, Cretan (Linear B), and Arabic. These Jews heard the mighty deeds of God proclaimed in their own adopted Gentile languages by speakers who had never learned those languages.

To those who did not share the language being spoken nearby, the phenomenon sounded like drunkenness — which is precisely what Isaiah had prophesied. Peter's corrective in Acts 2:15 was to distinguish the filling of the Spirit from intoxication and to anchor the phenomenon in Isaiah's prophecy. The content was always propositional: the gospel and the mighty deeds of God. There was no ecstatic gibberish. There was no unknown language. The word 'unknown' in the King James rendering of 1 Corinthians 14 is supplied by the translators in italics; the Greek text specifies only a foreign language — a real, structured, human language perfectly spoken by someone who had never learned it.

The same structural pattern appears in the Gentile Pentecost of Acts 10:44–46 and the transitional Pentecost of Acts 19:2–7. In every instance the function was identical: Jewish unbelievers were being warned by means of a Gentile language that the dispensational clock had turned.

IV. The Cessation of the Gift — 1 Corinthians 13:8–10

First Corinthians 13:8 states that spiritual gifts, including tongues, would be abolished. The verb is the future passive indicative of katargeō (καταργέω), meaning to abolish, to render inoperative, to bring to an end. The passive voice indicates that the gift itself receives the action of abolition; the indicative mood affirms this as historical reality.

Verse 10 specifies the terminus: when the completed has come. The key adjective is teleios (τέλειος). In the masculine and feminine genders teleios means perfect or complete; in the neuter gender, as used here, it means only complete — not perfect. The neuter adjective modifies an implied noun: the completed canon of Scripture. The reference is to the completion of the New Testament canon in AD 96. From that point forward, the text declares, the temporary gifts — including tongues — are abolished. The canon is itself the sufficient and final communication of doctrine; no supplementary sign gift is needed or authorized.

The gift of tongues was therefore operative for a precisely defined period: from the Day of Pentecost, June AD 30, to the administration of the fifth cycle of discipline against Israel in August AD 70. Within that window it functioned as a legitimate spiritual gift sovereignly bestowed by the Holy Spirit. After AD 70 it ceased as a legitimate gift. After AD 96, with the completion of the canon, the category of temporary sign gifts was formally and permanently closed.

V. Eight Characteristics of the Legitimate Gift During Its Tenure

First Corinthians 12–14 provides the complete biblical regulation of the gift during its legitimate period. Eight characteristics emerge from that passage.

1. Tongues was not necessary for salvation.

First Corinthians 12:3 states that no one can confess Jesus is Lord except through the Spirit — and this is set in the tongues context to clarify that tongues was not the vehicle of saving faith. Salvation has always been through non-meritorious faith in Christ alone.

2. Tongues was never assigned as the criterion of spirituality.

First Corinthians 12:11 states that the Spirit distributes gifts to each one individually as he sovereignly decides. The gift was sovereign; it could not be self-induced, manufactured, or transferred by human pressure.

3. Tongues must not be confused with the baptism of the Spirit.

First Corinthians 12:13 establishes that by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body — whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free. The baptism of the Spirit is universal among believers at salvation; the gift of tongues was particular, bestowed to some but not to all.

4. Tongues should not produce an inferiority complex in those without the gift.

First Corinthians 12:15–16 uses the body analogy. The foot is no less a member of the body because it is not the hand. The ear is no less a member because it is not the eye. The pattern of intimidation — you are not genuinely saved unless you speak in tongues — is condemned by the structure of the passage itself.

5. Tongues should not produce a superiority complex in those who possessed the gift.

First Corinthians 12:21: the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. The head — representing the Lord Jesus Christ — cannot say to the feet, I have no need of you. The body is interdependent and no member may despise another on the basis of its particular gift.

6. Tongues was the least of all spiritual gifts.

First Corinthians 12:28 lists the gifts in order of merit — the only such ranked list in Scripture. Apostles stand first, prophets second, teachers third, then miracles, gifts of healing, helps, administrations. Tongues — various kinds of foreign languages — appear last on the list. The gift that generated the most controversy and the loudest claims of superiority was in fact the gift of least rank.

7. Tongues was only effective when exercised under the filling of the Spirit.

First Corinthians 13 establishes love — functioning here as a metonymy for the filling of the Spirit — as the precondition for any spiritual gift to be effective. A tongues utterance made by a believer out of fellowship was spiritually valueless regardless of its linguistic accuracy.

8. The abuse of tongues during its tenure demanded strict regulation.

First Corinthians 14 devotes forty verses to the regulation of tongues in corporate worship. Tongues were identified as the inferior gift (verses 1–25); their abuse in the assembly required extensive controls (verses 26–35); and the governing principle was stated in verses 36–40: what matters is not tongues but response to doctrine.

VI. Post-Canonical Tongues as a Satanic Function

After AD 70, the legitimate gift of tongues ceased. After AD 96, the completion of the canon rendered every temporary sign gift permanently inoperative. What presents itself as tongues after those dates is not a continuation of a legitimate spiritual gift but a satanic counterfeit operating through two mechanisms: demon possession in unbelievers and demon influence in reversionistic believers.

The believer cannot be demon possessed because the Holy Spirit indwells his body at salvation. He can, however, be demon influenced — specifically through the channel of emotional reversionism, which opens the right lobe to demonic doctrine through the vacuum of the soul. The tongues phenomenon in a believer is the fruit of reversionism, not of the Spirit.

Second Thessalonians 2:7–12 describes the escalating satanic activity of the inter-advent period. The mystery of lawlessness is already at work. After the rapture removes the restraining ministry of the Spirit, the lawless one will be revealed, whose coming is according to the working of Satan with all power and attesting miracles and wonders of falsehood. The pseudo-miraculous — including counterfeit tongues — is part of this program of deception. Those deceived are described as those who do not receive the love of the truth so as to be delivered; God permits a deluding influence — an inworking of error — upon those who embrace what is false.

The mechanism of demonic vocal control is referenced in Isaiah 8:19 and 29:4, where a ventriloquist-type demon controls the vocal cords of a medium to produce speech. This is the structural parallel to what presents as tongues in the contemporary world. A demon-possessed unbeliever can, through demonic agency, produce foreign language utterances — which is why the phenomenon is not always simply gibberish. It is pseudo-tongues: structurally similar to the legitimate gift, but demonic in origin and purpose.

The command of Romans 16:17–18 — to separate from those who cause dissensions and apostasies by means of emotional manipulation — therefore applies directly to contemporary tongues advocates. Their appeal is always to emotion, not to doctrine. Their instrument is always smooth and flattering speech directed at the unsuspecting. Their effect is always the domination of the soul by emotion at the expense of the right lobe. Separation from them is not optional: it is part of the drill of the royal family honor code.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Five

1. Romans 16:19a opens with the inferential conjunction gar (γάρ), rendered 'certainly' to capture Paul's settled apostolic confidence. The report of the Roman believers' obedience — their authority orientation — has become widely known, and this is precisely what qualifies them to execute the drill of separation commanded in verse 17.

2. Authority orientation is the structural prerequisite for executing separation without sin. Impersonal love can separate from a believer cleanly — without bitterness, vindictiveness, or implacability — because it does not require the other person's cooperation or change. The believer who is authority-oriented understands that freedom and legitimate authority are not in conflict but are mutually constitutive of capacity for life.

3. The gift of tongues was a historically bounded, specifically purposed, sovereignly bestowed spiritual gift. Its purpose was to evangelize Jewish unbelievers in Gentile languages as a forty-year warning that the fifth cycle of discipline was approaching and that the dispensation of Israel had been suspended. It was not an ecstatic phenomenon, not a mark of spirituality, not a condition of salvation, and not available to all believers.

4. The Old Testament prophecy of Isaiah 28:11 is the doctrinal anchor for the gift of tongues. Paul quotes this text in 1 Corinthians 14:21–22 to establish that tongues was a sign to unbelieving Israel, not a blessing to the assembled church. Every generation of mature Old Testament believers who lived into the new dispensation could have predicted this development from the Mosaic and prophetic framework they already possessed.

5. The seven feasts of Israel encoded the entire structure of redemptive history, including the gap of the church age. The three-month interval between Pentecost and Trumpets was designed to represent the suspension of the age of Israel and the insertion of the church age. The gift of tongues was the living counterpart to that gap in the calendar: a sign that history had shifted and that no Jewish nation would again serve as client nation to God until the second advent.

6. The gift of tongues ceased in AD 70 with the fifth cycle of discipline against Israel, and was formally abolished at the completion of the canon in AD 96. First Corinthians 13:8 predicts abolition by the future passive of katargeō (καταργέω). Verse 10 locates the terminus at the completion — teleios (τέλειος) in the neuter, meaning 'complete' not 'perfect' — of the New Testament canon. No legitimate expression of the gift of tongues has occurred since AD 96.

7. Eight characteristics of the gift during its legitimate tenure establish the biblical controls against abuse. Tongues was not a condition of salvation; not a criterion of spirituality; not to be confused with the baptism of the Spirit; not a basis for inferiority in those without it; not a basis for superiority in those with it; the least of all gifts in rank; effective only under the filling of the Spirit; and subject to strict regulation in corporate worship.

8. Contemporary tongues is a satanic counterfeiting operation, not a continuation of a legitimate spiritual gift. Two mechanisms are involved: demon possession producing pseudo-linguistic utterances in unbelievers, and demon influence operating through emotional reversionism in believers. The ventriloquist-demon referenced in Isaiah 8:19 and 29:4 is the structural mechanism behind post-canonical tongues. The command of Romans 16:17 — separation — applies directly to those who propagate this phenomenon.

9. The doctrine of authority orientation, introduced in Romans 16:19a, provides the operational foundation for the remainder of Paul's concluding exhortation. It will be developed fully in the following chapter. Its appearance here is not incidental: Paul's confidence that the Roman believers can separate without sinning is rooted entirely in his recognition that they are already authority-oriented. The report of that orientation has reached everyone — and that is the apostle's basis for joy.

Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Six

Romans 16:19 — Authority Orientation and the Plan of God

Romans 16:19 “For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Certainly the report of your obedience — your authority orientation — has become known to all. Therefore, because of you, I am delighted. But I want you to be learned ones with reference to the good, and simple concerning evil.

Romans 16:19 stands at the culmination of Paul's letter to the Roman believers. Having addressed the problem of division-makers and apostasy-producers in verse 17, Paul now turns to commend the Roman congregations for a specific quality that has made them known throughout the Christian world: authority orientation. This chapter examines that commendation, the grammatical structure of Paul's rejoicing, and the technical theological content of the phrase 'wise with reference to the good' — a phrase whose full meaning is anchored in the plan of God as traced through Romans 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16.

I. The Commendation: Authority Orientation in Rome

Paul opens verse 19 with a causal affirmation: the report of the Roman believers' obedience has become known to all. The word 'obedience' in this context functions as a technical term for authority orientation — the voluntary alignment of the believer's will with divinely delegated structures of authority. This is confirmed by context: verse 17 warns against those who cause dissensions contrary to doctrine received from a teacher, and the contrast in verse 19 is between such divisive figures and the congregation that has remained steady under doctrinal authority.

At least three local churches are identifiable in Rome at the time Paul writes, approximately AD 68. The mature believers Paul addresses are distributed among these congregations. Their maturity is not accidental — it is traceable to two convergent causes: faithful and accurate doctrinal teaching by their pastors, and authority orientation on the part of the congregation. Both are required. Teaching without receptive authority orientation produces nothing; authority orientation without sound doctrine produces religious compliance without spiritual content.

It is significant that Paul's own pastoral authority is not directly at stake here. He is writing as an apostle, not as the local pastor of any Roman congregation. He has never met most of these believers face to face. His joy, therefore, is not the satisfaction of a pastor recovering lost ground, but the broader admiration of an apostle observing a congregation not his own that has advanced in the plan of God through the proper channels.

II. Paul's Rejoicing: Grammatical Analysis of the Opening Clause

The prepositional phrase opening Paul's response is constructed from the preposition followed by the genitive plural of the second-person personal pronoun, rendered literally 'because of you.' This is followed by a post-positive inferential particle that draws a conclusion from the preceding commendation.

The verb rendered 'I am delighted' is the present active indicative of chairō (χαίρω), meaning to rejoice, to be glad, to be delighted. The progressive present tense denotes action in a continuing state — Paul is not merely expressing a momentary response but a sustained disposition of joy. The active voice confirms Paul as the one producing the action. The declarative mood places this in the realm of historical reality. Corrected translation: Therefore, because of you, I am delighted.

Authority orientation is identified here as a blessing operating on two levels. First, it is a blessing to the believer himself, because it is a prerequisite for perception of Bible doctrine — the only means of advancing to maturity and receiving the imputation of divine blessing in time. Second, it is a blessing to others, because authority-oriented mature believers collectively form the pivot through which a national entity not only survives but sustains its prosperity under the plan of God.

III. Authority Orientation: Doctrinal Development

A. Freedom and Authority as Inseparable Categories

Freedom as a divinely established category is not a single principle but a compound of four interrelated concepts forming one category. These four are freedom itself — understood as self-determination — privacy, property, and authority. No one of these four can be attacked or destroyed without simultaneously dismantling the entire structure of freedom. They stand or fall together.

Freedom in its primary sense is the principle of divine establishment and honor code function. Privacy is the principle related to the honor code function of the believer's priesthood. Property is the principle related to the laws of divine establishment for the function of life. Authority is the umbrella concept — the structural canopy under which all human freedom exists and is protected.

An assault on property through redistribution of wealth or confiscation replaces freedom with tyranny. An assault on privacy — whether through institutional slavery on the one hand, or through the sin of gossip on the other — destroys the same category by different means. Both slavery and gossip are antithetical systems that converge on the same point of damage: the elimination of privacy, and with it, freedom.

Freedom itself is also lost through other channels: demon influence on the believer's thinking — which, while not possession, can shape the content of the soul in directions contrary to divine establishment — and through addiction to substances that compromise volition. Yet the most subtle and therefore the most dangerous assault on freedom originates not in these external forces, but in the rejection of either establishment or royal family authority. Authority is responsibility organized to protect freedom. Attack on authority is therefore irresponsibility organized to destroy it.

B. The Definition and Scope of Authority

Under the laws of divine establishment, authority is defined as the legal power delegated by God whereby certain members of the human race have jurisdiction and responsibility over all members of the human race, so that freedom might be guaranteed to all. The purpose of authority is always the preservation of freedom — specifically, the freedom of self-determination: the freedom to succeed, the freedom to fail, but always the guaranteed opportunity to choose.

The specific domains of divinely ordained authority include the four divine institutions: volition, marriage, family, and government. In the sphere of volition, authority resides in the soul of the individual through the faculty of free will. In marriage, authority is vested in the husband. In the family, authority belongs to parents over children. In government, authority must be held with corresponding responsibility — the function of government is to guarantee and protect freedom from crime and tyranny, not to engineer social outcomes through legislation. Social problems are not subject to legislative solution; legislation is designed to protect freedom, not to redistribute its results.

Additional spheres of authority include the academic institution, where the professor and administration hold authority over the student who is, by definition, a learner without portfolio. The student is present to receive instruction, not to administer it. Whether a student agrees with a school's policies is not the operative question; as long as he is enrolled, he is obligated to function within the authority structure he has voluntarily entered. Any institution has the right to establish its own policies from within its own authority.

In the economic sphere, authority rests with the investor and the executive who are accountable to those who have placed capital at risk. The authority of law enforcement — the police officer and judicial function — represents the last institutional line between the freedom of citizens and the chaos of anarchy. Military authority operates through rank and command structure, which is essential to operational effectiveness and cannot be compromised by social experimentation without destroying the institution's capacity to function.

C. Spiritual Authority and the Local Church

In the spiritual domain, divine authority is stated in the context of the Word of God and delegated to the communicator of the Word — the pastor of the local church. The pastor holds authority over the congregation within his sphere of ministry. The evangelist holds authority in the proclamation of the gospel to unbelievers. Both forms of authority are delegated within the framework of the local church, with full responsibility operative at every level.

Hebrews 13:17 provides the normative statement: Keep obeying those pastors who themselves are ruling over you and submit to their authority. For these same pastors keep watching for the benefit of your souls as those who have to render an account. Keep obeying them in order that they may do this accounting with joy, and not with groaning, for this would be unprofitable for you. The critical implication of this verse is that the pastor is accountable to the Lord, not to the congregation. This accountability structure is not a license for irresponsibility; it is the very mechanism that protects doctrinal integrity from the pressures of congregational preference.

The pastor's authority is limited to those within his sphere of ministry. In the present age, the communication media of tape, radio, and other means of transmission have extended that sphere so that a believer may receive consistent doctrinal teaching from a pastor he has never met in person — provided the ministry is consistent and the teaching is accurate. The principle of authority orientation applies equally in these extended contexts.

God has provided two umbrellas of authority over the mechanics of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP): a divine umbrella in the teaching ministry of God the Holy Spirit, who indwells every believer and must fill the person for perception to occur; and a human umbrella in the teaching function of the pastor of the local church. The pastor's personality is never the issue in authority orientation. Preoccupation with the communicator's personality is a distraction from the only relevant question: is doctrine being perceived and retained?

The academic discipline of the local church classroom includes no unnecessary talking or movement, and nothing that would break personal concentration or disturb others who are concentrating. These are not arbitrary formalities; they express the honor code of the royal family of God in its recognition of what common sense and good manners require — respect for the Word of God and thoughtfulness toward others who are there to learn.

The warning against tampering with the Lord's communicator has explicit Old Testament warrant in Isaiah 54:17: No weapon which is formed against you shall prosper, and every tongue which accuses you in judgment, you will condemn. This is the heritage of the servant of the Lord, and his vindication is from me, decrees Jehovah. Dissatisfaction with a pastor may arise for any number of reasons; the temptation to judge, malign, or discredit the Lord's communicator is a constant one. The warning of this passage is clear: vindication belongs to God, not to the congregation.

IV. 'Wise with Reference to the Good': Grammatical and Theological Analysis

A. The Grammar of Paul's Wish

Following the commendation and the expression of rejoicing, Paul introduces a contrast with a post-positive conjunctive particle, signaling a shift from what the Roman believers have achieved to what still requires attention.

The verb is the present active indicative of thelō (θέλω), expressing a wish or deliberate purpose. As an apostle, Paul's use of this verb carries the weight of apostolic authority. The progressive present indicates persistent desire: but I keep wanting you to be. The accusative plural direct object refers to all the believers in Rome. The infinitive of eimi (εἶναι) follows in the perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results — in this case, the results of sustained doctrinal intake. This is the infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and outcome.

The accusative plural of sophos (σοφός) — wise ones, learned ones, sagacious ones — governs the prepositional phrase that follows. The preposition eis (εἰς) plus the accusative singular of agathos (ἀγαθός) forms a technical expression: wise with reference to the good. In the Epistle to the Romans, agathos in this technical sense refers specifically to the plan of God.

B. The Good as the Plan of God: X + Y + Z

The technical use of 'the good' as a reference to the plan of God appears at multiple strategic points throughout Romans, establishing a consistent pattern that reaches its climax here in 16:19.

Romans 8:28 introduces the formula: We know in fact that to those who love God — occupation with the person of Christ — all things work together for the purpose of the good, to those who are the called ones according to a predetermined plan. The plan of God is here expressed as X + Y + Z, a three-stage framework of divine provision covering the entirety of the believer's existence from regeneration through eternity.

In the X-axis of the plan, human life is imputed at birth — not at conception, where only biological activity exists. The moment of imputation of human life establishes the purpose of God for that individual. Simultaneously, the imputation of Adam's original sin establishes instant condemnation, which in turn establishes the basis for instant salvation when faith in Christ is exercised. This arrangement also guarantees that those who die before reaching accountability — including those who never develop cognitive capacity — go directly to heaven, because their condemnation was judicial rather than personal. The first potential of the plan is therefore salvation, available to every member of the human race.

The first hope — elpis (ἐλπίς) — is absolute confidence that the one who believes in Jesus Christ possesses eternal life. Salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ is the first plus that completes the X-axis and transitions the believer into the Y-axis of the plan.

In the Y-axis, two judicial imputations operate. First, all the sins of the world were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. Second, the righteousness of God was imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ. These two judicial imputations establish the second potential of the plan: the glorification of God in time through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The pertinent doctrine required for this potential is the full scope of Bible doctrine as perceived through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

The second hope is absolute confidence that when the believer cracks the maturity barrier, blessing from God is imputed in six categories, and this imputation of blessing constitutes the basis for glorifying God in time and for resolving the tactical dimension of the angelic conflict. Maturity adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in the soul is the second plus, replacing the hope with reality and transitioning the believer into the Z-axis.

In the Z-axis, eternal life imputed at salvation is combined with blessing imputed at maturity and thereafter, establishing the third potential: great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. The third hope is absolute confidence that those who crack the maturity barrier and maintain their advance will receive incomparable blessing in eternity. This entire framework — X + Y + Z — is what 'the good' designates in Romans.

C. The Good Traced Through Romans

Romans 12:2: Stop being conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renovation of your thought, that you may prove what the will of God is — namely, the good. The will of God is the good — momentum and advance in the plan of God.

Romans 12:9: Your love must be non-hypocritical; despise the evil, adhere to the good. The opposition between evil and the good is categorical — they represent the policy of Satan as the ruler of this world versus the plan of God.

Romans 12:21: Stop being conquered by evil, but conquer evil by the good. Advance in the plan of God is the operative means by which evil is overcome.

Romans 13:4: For it — human government — is a minister of God to you for the purpose of the good. The laws of divine establishment, administered through legitimate governmental authority, sponsor the spiritual advance of the believer by providing the freedom necessary for the function of the priesthood and ambassadorship.

Romans 14:16: Let not the good attained by you be slandered. The good — the advance of the believer in the plan of God — must not be jeopardized by divisive conduct or compromise.

Romans 15:2: Let each one of us, mature believers, accommodate his neighbor — the one in his periphery — for the purpose of the good: advancing to maturity. Accommodation of the weaker believer is itself an expression of mature advance in the plan of God.

Romans 16:19 completes the pattern: 'I want you to be wise with reference to the good.' Understanding the plan of God and its objective is the sum of what Paul desires for the Roman believers. This understanding has specific practical implications.

D. Principles Governing Wisdom with Reference to the Good

Several principles flow from the technical content of agathos as the plan of God in this verse:

Understanding the plan of God and its objective eliminates involvement with evil, which is the policy of Satan as the ruler of this world. The believer who comprehends the structure and goal of X + Y + Z has no need to pursue the counterfeit satisfactions that the world system offers.

Momentum in the plan of God depends on doctrine resident in the soul. There is no alternative mechanism. Bible doctrine perceived, retained, and applied is the only fuel for sustained spiritual advance.

Doctrine resident in the soul, when applied to circumstances, eliminates the energy of the flesh as a modus operandi. Operation in the energy of the flesh detracts from the attainment of the objectives God designed for each believer in eternity past.

Motivation in the plan of God likewise depends on doctrine resident in the soul. The three hopes — the absolute confidence structures built into X, Y, and Z — provide motivation that cannot be generated by any other means.

Doctrine resident in the soul defines honor code principles and produces royal family integrity. Royal family integrity avoids compromise with good and evil alike — it neither embraces the world system nor dilutes the plan of God with human sentiment.

Therefore the believer can only be wise or sagacious about the plan of God through consistent and daily perception of Bible doctrine. There is no shortcut, no substitute, and no accelerant other than the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

The plan of God excludes involvement in social action, the welfare state, socialism, and the distortion of legislation to solve social problems — all forms of evil that distract the believer from the function of his priesthood and his ambassadorship. The believer's contribution to the nation is not social activism but the formation of the pivot: mature believers whose doctrinal orientation sustains divine blessing on the national entity.

The second half of verse 19 — 'and simple concerning evil' — introduces the antithetical concept that will be developed in detail in the next study.

Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Thirty-Six

1. Authority orientation is a prerequisite for spiritual advance. The positive believer advancing toward maturity through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception cannot maintain motivation or momentum apart from authority orientation. This is not a peripheral virtue but a structural necessity built into the mechanics of doctrinal perception.

2. Freedom is a four-part category, not a single principle. Freedom, privacy, property, and authority are interrelated concepts forming one category. An attack on any one of the four is an attack on all four. Authority, as the umbrella concept, is the most subtle target because its removal is often framed as an expansion of freedom rather than its destruction.

3. The most subtle attack on freedom originates in rejection of authority. External threats — demon influence, substance addiction — are less dangerous than the internal rejection of divinely ordained authority structures. Authority is responsibility organized for the protection of freedom; its rejection is irresponsibility organized for freedom's destruction.

4. Authority is delegated, not inherent. Under the laws of divine establishment, authority is the legal power delegated by God to specific members of the human race for the purpose of guaranteeing freedom to all. The domains of this delegation include volition, marriage, family, government, the academic institution, the economic enterprise, law enforcement, the military, and the local church.

5. The pastor's authority is limited to his congregation and is directed toward doctrinal communication. Hebrews 13:17 establishes that the pastor is accountable to the Lord, not to the congregation. This structure protects doctrinal integrity. The personality of the communicator is never the issue; the content of what is communicated is the only relevant question.

6. God provides two umbrellas of authority over the function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception. The divine umbrella is the teaching ministry of God the Holy Spirit, who must fill the believer for perception to occur. The human umbrella is the teaching function of the pastor. Both are required; neither is sufficient without the other.

7. The technical term 'the good' in Romans designates the plan of God expressed as X + Y + Z. This framework covers the full arc of the believer's existence: salvation adjustment to the justice of God (X), maturity adjustment to the justice of God (Y), and the great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ (Z). The three hopes correspond to the three stages and provide the motivational structure for advance.

8. Momentum in the plan of God depends entirely on doctrine resident in the soul. There is no alternative. Doctrine perceived through the Grace Apparatus for Perception, retained in the right lobe, and applied under the filling of the Holy Spirit is the only mechanism for sustained spiritual advance, maintained motivation, and the formation of the pivot.

9. The plan of God excludes social action and legislative solutions to social problems. The believer's unique contribution to the nation operates through the priesthood and ambassadorship, not through political or social activism. Social problems are not subject to legislative solution. The pivot of mature believers is the only mechanism through which sustained national blessing under the plan of God is maintained.

10. Authority orientation produces joy in the apostle. Paul's use of the present active indicative of chairō (χαίρω) expresses a sustained, ongoing delight in the authority orientation of the Roman believers. This joy is not pastoral propriety but the genuine response of the spiritually mature to observing the plan of God working through the proper channels in a congregation he has never personally shepherded.
